Explanation:
This is a flaw question, so the right answer has to name the specific defect in how the columnist moves from evidence to conclusion, not merely something the argument leaves out.

The conclusion comes first: the medical press greatly exaggerates the dangers of drinking. The only support offered is a single case, the columnist's grandfather, who drank heavily for a lifetime and reached 95. Notice what the medical claim actually is. It is a general claim about a tendency across a population, that alcohol can shorten life. A claim of that shape is perfectly compatible with individual exceptions; no one asserts that every heavy drinker dies young.

So before you read the choices, expect something like one unrepresentative case cannot overturn a claim about a general tendency. That is exactly the mismatch here: the columnist sets a lone family story against population-level evidence and declares the evidence overblown.
explanation_A: Moral objections to drinking are nowhere in play. The medical press, as the columnist describes it, makes a health claim about shortened lifespans, and the columnist disputes that health claim. An argument is not flawed for ignoring a question it never raised, so this is simply out of scope.
explanation_B: This is the trap. It sounds like the familiar alternative-cause criticism, and students reach for it because the grandfather's long life surely had other contributing factors. But look at who needs that point. The columnist is not explaining why his grandfather lived so long; he is using the grandfather to deny a general tendency. Other life-shortening factors would matter if a cause were being assigned. The reasoning breaks down one step earlier, at the leap from a single case to a population-wide claim.
explanation_C: Quality of life versus length of life is a real distinction, but it is not the one the argument turns on. The medical claim under attack is explicitly about alcohol shortening lives, and the grandfather evidence is offered on that same dimension. Faulting the columnist for ignoring quality criticizes his choice of topic rather than his inference.
explanation_D: Cause and effect are not reversed anywhere here. That flaw would require treating a result as its own source, concluding for instance that ill health drives heavy drinking rather than the other way round. The columnist makes no such swap; he offers one long-lived relative as a counterweight to the medical literature. This is the wrong flaw, picked off a list.
explanation_E: Correct. The medical press is described as making a broad claim about alcohol's effect on lifespan, and the columnist answers it with exactly one person he happens to know. That is anecdote against aggregate. A claim about what alcohol tends to do leaves room for individuals who drink heavily and still live long, so producing one such individual does nothing to show the claim is exaggerated. Notice too that the columnist cannot rule out that his grandfather would have lived longer still without the drinking.

Explanation:
The stem asks how the argument proceeds, so your job is to describe the move rather than judge it. The right answer has to match both the charge being answered and the way the author answers it.

Separate the pieces. Others charge that using food crops for fuel is an unprecedented attack on the food supply, and they add that diverting crops looks immoral while people need food. The author concedes nothing about morality. He introduces one fact instead: crops are already diverted away from human food, to feed livestock. From that he concludes only that fuel diversion is not a radical break with traditional practice.

So the target is the word unprecedented, and the tool is a parallel case that is already accepted. Expect an answer saying the author meets a charge of radicalism by pointing to an existing practice of the same kind. Watch for choices that have him defending the practice morally; he leaves that half of the charge untouched.
explanation_A: Nothing is weighed against anything. A consequence-balancing argument would have to grant harms from diverting food to fuel and then claim larger offsetting benefits, such as energy security or lower emissions. No benefit of fuel crops is ever mentioned. The author's whole contribution is the observation about livestock feed, which speaks to precedent rather than to any ledger of good and bad effects.
explanation_B: Here the author would be denying that the alleged consequence occurs, arguing that food crops used for fuel do not actually reduce the food supply. He concedes the opposite. Diversion is real; his point is that we already do it for animals. Denying a consequence and claiming precedent for it are different moves, and only the second appears in this paragraph.
explanation_C: Correct. The charge the author picks out is that the practice is unprecedented, a radical break, and his answer is the livestock case: crops are already pulled from the human food supply for another use that no one calls revolutionary. Because the two practices share the feature the charge rests on, edible crops going somewhere other than people, the new practice is cast as more of the same rather than a departure. The conclusion is pitched at exactly that level, denying a radical break and claiming nothing further.
explanation_D: Tempting, because the stimulus does raise the thought that diverting crops seems immoral. But trace the conclusion. It is about tradition and radicalism, not about right and wrong, and the livestock comparison is never turned against the moral principle behind the objection. If anything the author lets the moral charge stand and narrows his target. Picking this means reading the conclusion a step stronger than it was written.
explanation_E: This reverses the argument twice over. The author is resisting a moral objection rather than supporting one, and his method is to show that the practice is like an accepted one, not that it differs from practices which merely seem similar. Every directional term in the choice points the wrong way.

Explanation:
This is a point at issue question. The correct answer has to be a claim one speaker asserts and the other denies; agreement, silence, or a difference in emphasis all disqualify a choice.

Hernandez argues from a fact about audiences to a prescription: because people give celebrity opinions extra weight, debates get warped, so celebrities should stay out of controversial issues where they lack expertise. Liu does not challenge the fact. He explicitly grants that people give celebrities' opinions more credence than they should, denies that this is the celebrities' fault, and concludes that it is absurd for them not to feel free to join such debates.

The conflict therefore sits entirely at the level of the recommendation. Before scanning the choices, expect the disagreement to be the prescription itself: Hernandez says refrain, Liu says speak. The factual premises are shared ground, so any choice restating them is a trap.
explanation_A: Both speakers sign on to this. Hernandez states it outright as the reason debates get warped, and Liu repeats it when he concedes that people give celebrities' opinions more credence than they should. Shared premises cannot be the point at issue, and this is the clearest piece of common ground in the exchange.
explanation_B: Correct, and it is Hernandez's conclusion nearly intact: celebrities should avoid speaking publicly on controversial matters outside their expertise. Liu's closing sentence denies precisely that, calling it absurd that celebrities should not feel free to join controversial debates. One says refrain, the other says free to speak, about the same people and the same debates. Notice that Liu arrives at the opposite prescription without disputing any of Hernandez's facts, which is what makes this the point of conflict rather than their shared observation about audiences.
explanation_C: Hernandez does assert the warping effect, so half the test is met. Liu, though, never takes a position on it. His reply concedes the audience behaviour and shifts to blame and entitlement, arguing that the distortion is not the celebrity's doing. Silence from the second speaker is not disagreement, and a point at issue needs both speakers on record.
explanation_D: Neither speaker tells the public what to do. Hernandez addresses his recommendation to celebrities, and Liu's rejoinder defends celebrities' freedom to speak. This might be a plausible further position for Hernandez, but inferring what someone would probably also think is not identifying what they said, and Liu is equally unrecorded on it.
explanation_E: Liu does deny this, saying it is not the celebrities' fault that people overweight their opinions. A disagreement needs Hernandez to affirm it, and he does not. He treats the extra credence as something the public does, then draws a conclusion about how celebrities ought to respond to that fact, never about who is to blame for it. One speaker on record is not enough.

Explanation:
A resolve the discrepancy question hands you two facts that sit badly together and asks for a third that lets both stand. The right answer explains the puzzling result without denying either statement.

Lay out the tension. A decaffeination process exists that removes caffeine without seriously compromising taste. Yet when decaffeinated coffee first reached the market, many drinkers found it tasted rather bad. Notice the hidden assumption that creates the puzzle: that the only thing determining how the finished coffee tastes is the process applied to it. Taste also depends on what goes into the pot in the first place.

So prephrase something that locates the bad flavour somewhere other than decaffeination. If the beans themselves were poor, the process could leave taste essentially untouched and the product could still taste bad, because there was little good taste there to preserve. Both reports then hold at once and the discrepancy dissolves.
explanation_A: Market share today tells you nothing about why early decaf tasted bad. This compares the proportion of decaf-only drinkers now with the proportion back then, which at most hints that the product later improved. The discrepancy concerns the original complaints, and a subsequent trend neither explains them nor squares them with the claim made for the process.
explanation_B: Willingness to drink is a separate matter from flavour. This says some coffee drinkers would avoid decaf even granting that it tastes as good as regular, which points to a preference for caffeine or to habit. The puzzle is that people who did drink it reported bad taste. Explaining a refusal unrelated to taste leaves those complaints exactly as unexplained as before.
explanation_C: Accompanying foods can affect how any coffee tastes, and that is precisely the weakness: the point applies just as much to regular coffee. A factor that hits both sides evenly cannot explain why decaffeinated coffee in particular drew complaints. Resolving this discrepancy requires something that distinguishes the decaf of that period from the coffee people were already drinking.
explanation_D: Price is not flavour. A higher cost might explain slow adoption or resentment, and a student can talk themselves into a story in which expectations raised by the price produce disappointment at the first sip. That story is doing all the work, not the choice. Nothing here connects cost to how the coffee actually tasted, so the two statements stay in tension.
explanation_E: Correct. The claim made for the process is narrow: it removes caffeine without seriously compromising the coffee's taste. That promises only that the coffee tastes much as it did going in. If processors in those years used only low-quality beans for their decaffeinated products, what went in tasted bad already, and a process that faithfully preserves taste will deliver a bad-tasting cup. Both statements hold together, with the flavour problem traced to the raw material rather than to decaffeination.

Explanation:
This is a weaken question, so the correct answer attacks the link between evidence and conclusion without having to disprove anything the researchers observed.

The evidence: eighteen subjects were paid to lie about a playing card, and while lying their scans showed increased activity in brain regions known to respond to stress. The conclusion: fMRI could eventually underpin an effective lie detector. The unstated requirement is discrimination. A detector is worthless unless the signal it reads appears when someone lies and is absent, or clearly weaker, when someone tells the truth. The study only ever examined the lying condition; it never reports what truthful subjects' brains were doing.

So the prephrase writes itself: show that the same stress signal turns up in people telling the truth. Then the marker the researchers found cannot sort liars from honest subjects, and the proposal loses its basis even though every observed fact still stands.
explanation_A: If existing methods such as the polygraph are unreliable, that argues for seeking a better technique, not against this one. The conclusion concerns what fMRI might eventually achieve, and the shortcomings of a different technology leave it untouched. Readers sometimes treat general scepticism about lie detection as damaging; here it points, if anywhere, in the author's favour.
explanation_B: What most people think about the ethics of lying in an experiment has no bearing on whether brain activity distinguishes lies from truth. If anything, a sense of wrongdoing would heighten the very stress response the researchers measured, which supports the finding rather than undermining it. This is a comment on the subjects' attitudes, not on the inference.
explanation_C: The most attractive wrong answer. Wide variation in how much stress a lie produces does complicate calibration, and you can see a practical obstacle. But variation in degree is survivable: a usable detector could compare a person against their own baseline, and the choice still concedes that lying brings stress. What it never claims is that truthful people show the same reaction, which is the fatal problem. A difficulty of degree is much weaker than a failure of kind.
explanation_D: Contrasting planned with spontaneous lies suggests the signal is smaller in some cases, which chips at the proposal only at the edges. Note too that these subjects were instructed in advance, so their lies were closer to the planned variety and still produced the stress response. The choice identifies a complication to work around rather than removing the basis for the conclusion.
explanation_E: Correct. The argument's entire support is that lying produced stress-related activity. If truthful subjects show similar stress reactions in the brain, that activity no longer marks out lying at all, and a machine reading it would flag honest people exactly as it flags liars. Nothing in the study is contradicted; the increased activity still happened. What disappears is the contrast any detector needs, which is why this choice goes after the conclusion rather than the data.

Explanation:
A necessary assumption is something the argument cannot do without. Test candidates by negation: if denying the choice leaves the reasoning in ruins, it was required.

Officials deny that their policies produced serious environmental degradation; the author says the facts show otherwise. His facts form a sequence. The government repealed a long-standing ban on dumping mining wastes into streams, and since the repeal hundreds of miles of streams have been buried under those wastes. The conclusion is causal, that the policy produced the damage, while the evidence establishes only that the damage followed the policy.

That gap is the whole question. For the repeal to have produced the burials, the world without the repeal has to look different. Expect an answer saying that had the ban survived, far less waste would have reached the streams. Negate it and the dumping would have happened anyway, leaving the officials right and the author with nothing.
explanation_A: Why the government acted is beside the point. The author mentions the mining companies' urging in passing, but his case would run identically had the repeal come from a change of heart or a budget dispute. An assumption that the companies were indispensable to the decision concerns political causes upstream of the policy, not whether the policy caused the environmental harm.
explanation_B: Sincerity is not at issue. The author says the facts show otherwise, which rebuts the officials' claim whether they believe it or not. Negate this and suppose the officials are perfectly honest; the streams are still buried and the argument stands unchanged. Attacking a speaker's good faith is a different project from showing that what they say is false.
explanation_C: Matching the companies that lobbied with the companies that dumped would make a tidier story, but the reasoning needs no such overlap. If other firms took advantage of the repeal and buried the streams, the policy change still produced the degradation, which is all the conclusion claims. A detail that would add colour is not a detail the argument depends on.
explanation_D: A general ranking of the government's responsiveness to industry against environmentalists is a broad political claim, and necessary assumptions are usually narrow. This argument concerns one repeal and its aftermath. Deny the choice and let the government be scrupulously even-handed as a rule; this particular ban was still lifted and these streams were still buried.
explanation_E: Correct, and the negation test makes it unmistakable. The author infers from timing that repealing the ban caused the burials. Suppose instead that roughly as much waste would have reached the streams with the ban in place, perhaps because it went unenforced or because companies would have dumped regardless. Then the repeal changed nothing, the damage cannot be laid at the policy's door, and the officials' denial survives. The argument therefore requires that a surviving ban would have kept considerably more waste out of the streams.

Explanation:
This is a strengthen question. You want the choice that best supports the critic's position, which here is not the correlation itself but the gloss the critic puts on it.

The reported pattern is that the more famous the concert pianist, the more pleasure the audience takes. The critic adds two things: that this is only fair, and that it gives no cause for cynicism about audiences' ability to tell good playing from bad. The cynical reading he is resisting is that listeners respond to the name rather than the performance, enjoying a concert because the pianist is celebrated.

To block that reading you need fame and quality to line up. If famous pianists are famous because they play better, then audiences taking more pleasure in famous performers is just audiences taking more pleasure in better playing, and their judgment is vindicated rather than impugned. Carry that prephrase into the choices.
explanation_A: Correct. The worry the critic dismisses is that greater pleasure at famous names shows audiences cannot judge playing. If fame usually reflects a pianist's talent, the correlation has an innocent explanation: the more famous performer is generally the better performer, so an audience enjoying the famous pianist more is tracking quality rather than reputation. It also makes good on the critic's claim that the pattern is only fair, since the extra pleasure is then earned. This supplies the bridge between fame and merit that his view requires.
explanation_B: This cuts the other way. If some of the finest pianists are unknown to the general public, fame and quality come apart, and the audience's preference for famous performers starts to look like exactly the misjudgment the critic denies. A student may read it as a harmless concession about obscure talents, but its force is to loosen the fame-to-talent link the critic depends on.
explanation_C: Audience size is the wrong variable. The critic's claim concerns how much pleasure listeners take and whether that pleasure reflects discernment. That famous pianists draw bigger crowds follows almost by definition from being famous, and says nothing about quality or about what the listeners in those seats can distinguish.
explanation_D: Inconsistency across performances is true of nearly every performer and does not touch the question. If anything, the suggestion that a great pianist may play poorly on a given night makes an audience's steady extra pleasure at famous names look less responsive to the actual playing. Either way the choice offers the critic no support.
explanation_E: Works that audiences find hard to appreciate would predict less pleasure at the very best pianists' concerts, which pulls against the reported pattern and against the critic's benign explanation of it. It also drives a wedge between playing well and pleasing listeners, the last thing the critic wants. Read carefully, this is a weakener.

Explanation:
The passage breaks off after since, so you are supplying the premise that makes the conclusion follow most strongly. Treat it as a strengthen question with the answer slotted into the argument itself.

Here is the chain. Mites of several species were trapped in rocks in a high-altitude cave and dated to about 2,000 years ago. Those same species are absent from the area around the cave today but live a few miles away where it is cooler. The conclusion is that the cave area was probably cooler 2,000 years ago.

That follows only if where these mites live is governed by climate. Suppose instead they are fussy about moisture, or rock type, or moved for reasons no one can name; then their old location tells you nothing about old temperatures. So prephrase a premise tying the species to narrow climatic requirements. With it in place, their presence at the cave back then means the cave then offered conditions they now find only in the cooler area.
explanation_A: Correct. The inference runs from where a species lives to what the climate was, and that step needs the species to work as a climate indicator. If these mites can survive only in very specific climates, their present range marks out those conditions, which today exist in the cooler area a few miles off rather than around the cave. Their presence at the cave 2,000 years ago therefore implies the cave area then matched the conditions they require, that is, it was cooler than it is now. The premise converts a change of location into a record of temperature.
explanation_B: A wetter climate in the cooler area actively hurts the argument. It supplies a rival explanation for why the mites live there now and not by the cave, namely moisture rather than temperature. The conclusion singles out cooling, so adding a competing variable makes that conclusion less secure, not more.
explanation_C: Attractive at first, because it sounds as though it tightens the dating. Consider what it actually adds: that the mites had not been living near the cave long before they were trapped. The argument needs no claim about how long they had been there, only that they were there then and are not there now. Ruling out an earlier residence narrows the history without connecting the mites to temperature at all, and that link is what the conclusion is missing.
explanation_D: Altitude is not temperature, and this points away from the conclusion. The cave is already described as high-altitude, so a species restricted to high elevations would have no trouble living there now, which makes its disappearance harder to explain by cooling. It also fails to account for the mites thriving a few miles away unless that site is high too, a connection the choice never makes.
explanation_E: A decline in the number of mite species near the cave restates the puzzle rather than explaining it. You already know these species are gone from the area. Learning that overall diversity is lower gives no reason to attribute the change to temperature instead of drought, predators, human disturbance or anything else.

Explanation:
Another resolve the discrepancy question: find the fact that lets both halves of the information be true at once. You are not after the most interesting claim about car buyers, only the one that dissolves the conflict.

The two halves are these. Shoppers say, and studies confirm, that reliability is their first priority, where a reliable model very rarely breaks down and needs no more maintenance than average. Yet some of the most reliable models sell poorly to those very shoppers. Notice the quiet gap: the studies describe actual reliability, measured after the fact, while a shopper standing in a showroom has to act on a belief about reliability.

So prephrase a mismatch between the two. If buyers judge reliability by something that can lag behind the facts, they can sincerely chase reliability and still pass over the models that currently deserve the label. No one is behaving irrationally, and nothing in the market studies has to be wrong.
explanation_A: Comparing reliability with fuel efficiency among shoppers' stated priorities just reinforces the first half of the puzzle. It tells you again that buyers say reliability matters most, which is the claim that makes their behaviour surprising in the first place. A choice that deepens a premise cannot discharge the tension that premise creates.
explanation_B: Correct. The discrepancy turns on the difference between a model being reliable and a model being believed reliable. Buyers cannot inspect a breakdown record from the lot, so they go on reputation, and reputation is built out of earlier model years. A manufacturer whose cars have genuinely improved still carries the old name, so sincere reliability-seekers steer away from models that now top the rankings. The market studies and the sales pattern both hold, with the lag between performance and perception accounting for the gap.
explanation_C: Owners keeping reliable cars for their full life concerns people who already bought, not shoppers choosing between models. It might explain a thin used-car supply or infrequent repeat purchases, but the puzzle is why buyers who prize reliability pass over the most reliable models on offer. The choice never speaks to that decision.
explanation_D: Worth slowing down on. Models that rarely break down yet demand a lot of maintenance fail the definition given, which requires both rare breakdowns and no more maintenance than average, so they are not among the most reliable models at all. The choice describes a group sitting outside the puzzle. What needs explaining is models that meet the full definition and still sell badly to reliability-minded buyers.
explanation_E: That some of the most stylish cars are unreliable explains why a buyer tempted by looks might end up with a bad car. It does not explain the stated pattern, in which people whose priority is reliability bypass the models that are most reliable. To make it help, you would have to assume those buyers are secretly driven by style, which contradicts the premise rather than reconciling it.

Explanation:
This is a complete-the-argument question, which is an inference question in disguise. The blank sits after "Therefore," so the right answer is whatever the two preceding sentences actually force - not the most interesting observation you could make about sleep.

You get two pieces. First, a reported finding: most individuals believe they sleep less than most other people do. Second, a logical fact the author supplies himself: it cannot be the case that most people sleep less than most other people. That second sentence is the engine. It does not say any one person's belief is impossible; it says the belief cannot be true of most people at once, since "less than most others" is a comparison that only a minority can win.

Lay those together. A majority holds a belief that a majority cannot hold truly, so some of those believers must be mistaken. Before reading the choices, prephrase something like: at least some people are wrong about sleeping less than others. Notice how modest that is - it supports some and nothing stronger, and it identifies the error as a false belief, not as ignorance of one's own sleep.
explanation_A: This choice says people hold beliefs that could not possibly be true even in principle. Watch the shift. What is impossible is the aggregate state of affairs - most people all sleeping less than most others. Any single person's belief that she sleeps less than most others is perfectly possible; plenty of individuals really do. So the beliefs at issue are false for some believers, not impossible in principle, and this choice misdescribes the very impossibility the second sentence establishes.
explanation_B: Here the claim is that most people do not know how much they sleep. Nothing in the stimulus concerns self-knowledge of sleep quantity. A person could track her own hours precisely and still be wrong about where they fall relative to everyone else, because the error lives in the comparison, not in the measurement. The choice also overshoots to most when the premises license only some.
explanation_C: This is the strongest trap. It keeps the comparative framing and correctly senses that people are getting something wrong, so it feels like the answer. The killer is the quantifier combined with direction. From "most believe it" plus "it cannot be true of most," you can conclude only that some believers err - a majority holding the belief minus the minority who hold it truly. The stimulus gives you no count that reaches most, and "underestimate how much they sleep" also slides from a false comparison into a misjudgment of one's own hours.
explanation_D: The subject changes here from a comparison to a standard. Thinking you sleep less than other people is a descriptive claim about rank; thinking you do not sleep as much as you should is a normative claim about sufficiency. The stimulus never mentions how much sleep anyone needs or ought to get, so this conclusion draws on material that simply is not there.
explanation_E: Correct. This is exactly what the two sentences force. Most individuals believe they sleep less than most other people, and the author establishes that this cannot be true of most people - the comparison is one only a minority can satisfy. So the believing majority must contain people whose belief is false. That gives you some people who incorrectly believe they sleep less than most others. The quantifier is right, the error is correctly located in the belief rather than in self-knowledge, and the content stays on the exact comparison the study measured.

Explanation:
This is a weaken question, so the correct answer does not have to refute Ross outright. It only has to make his conclusion less likely by undermining some step he needs. Start by getting the conclusion exactly right, because it has two halves and students routinely attack only one of them.

Ross concludes that making dramatists and performers honored government employees is an effective strategy for controlling theater and satisfying the public. His support: past repression has failed because people want theater for entertainment and harshly treated dramatists find subtle ways to criticize; and dramatists will not criticize governments that honor and employ them. So the plan is supposed to kill the criticism, since employees stay quiet, while still keeping theater available to a public that wants it.

The vulnerable half is the second one. Ross assumes that theater produced by government employees will still satisfy the public's appetite for entertainment. Prephrase along those lines before you read on: something that shows the audience will not accept this theater. That leaves the control half intact and attacks the half Ross simply assumed.
explanation_A: Cost of employment is a practical obstacle to adopting the strategy, not evidence that the strategy fails when adopted. Ross is making a conditional claim about what would work, and a government unwilling to pay for it has told you nothing about whether the plan would control theater or please the public. Keep feasibility and effectiveness apart; weaken questions reward the second.
explanation_B: This says unregulated theater rarely brings a government down. That speaks to whether control is worth pursuing, not to whether Ross's method of achieving it works. Ross never claims theater topples governments - only that it has subversive power governments have tried to suppress. Removing the motive for the policy leaves his reasoning about the policy untouched.
explanation_C: A genuinely tempting choice, because harsh treatment is part of Ross's story about why repression backfires. But read what the choice actually reports: criticism happening where governments are not harsh. That bears on the harsh-treatment half of his explanation, and even there only mildly. Ross's recommendation rests on a different premise, that dramatists will not criticize a government of which they are honored employees, and the choice says nothing at all about employed dramatists. The proposal survives untouched.
explanation_D: The claim that most productions are politically neutral addresses volume, not Ross's mechanism. Ross cares about the subversive minority, and neutral plays are exactly the ones his plan does not need to suppress. This also leaves the public-satisfaction half of his conclusion completely alone, which is where the argument is thin.
explanation_E: Correct, and it strikes the half of the conclusion Ross never defended. His plan is supposed to control theater and satisfy the public. If audiences generally dislike plays written or performed by government employees, then staffing the theater with honored employees produces exactly the plays the public will not watch. The entertainment appetite that made repression fail in the first place goes unmet, so the strategy loses the very feature that was supposed to make it succeed where outlawing theater did not.

Explanation:
This is a most-strongly-supported question. There is no conclusion to evaluate - just facts to combine - and the right answer is the claim those facts best underwrite, not merely one they leave open. Inventory them before you look at the choices.

First, many hikers carry cell phones for emergencies in remote areas. Second, many also phone wildlife offices when they see poachers breaking game laws, and agents arrive before the lawbreakers leave. Read that second fact carefully: it reports that these sightings actually happen. Third, poachers avoid areas they know hikers frequent.

Now put the second and third together. Poachers are being seen by hikers, yet poachers stay away from places they know hikers go. Both can be true only if the encounters occur somewhere outside the poachers' knowledge - areas hikers use but poachers do not recognize as hiker territory. Prephrase it as: hikers must be walking in some places poachers have not identified as hiker ground. Anything about trends in poaching rates, the cost of phones, or how effective this tactic is compared with others goes beyond what three static facts can deliver.
explanation_A: Affordability never comes up. The stimulus reports that many hikers carry phones, which tells you about behavior, not about the finances of hikers as a group - "many" does not establish what most can afford, and nothing fixes the price or anyone's budget. This is a plausible real-world guess being smuggled in as an inference.
explanation_B: A trend claim requires data over time, and you have none. The stimulus describes what happens when hikers spot poachers; it never says how often that happens, how many poachers there were before, or whether the deterrent effect simply relocates poaching rather than reducing it. Notice too that poachers avoiding hiker areas is consistent with them poaching just as much elsewhere.
explanation_C: What agents carry is simply absent from the stimulus. All you are told is that calls to wildlife offices get agents to the scene in time, which says nothing about the equipment in their pockets. If anything, the facts suggest the communication chain works; they certainly do not support a negative claim about agents' phones.
explanation_D: Correct, and it is forced by holding two facts side by side. Hikers do in fact see poachers breaking game laws - the stimulus says so in reporting the calls that bring agents to the scene. But poachers steer clear of areas they know hikers frequent. If poachers knew every area hikers use, these sightings could not be occurring. So at least some hikers must be in areas poachers do not know to be hiker-frequented. That is a modest some statement, which is exactly the strength three facts like these can support.
explanation_E: Tempting because the stimulus does describe phones helping catch poachers, and the story has a satisfying shape. The phrase that kills it is "one of the most effective tools." That is a comparative ranking, and the stimulus never mentions any other anti-poaching method, let alone measures this one against it. Supported-inference answers almost never require you to rate something against unmentioned alternatives.

Explanation:
This is a method-of-argument question. You are not judging whether the author is right; you are describing the move he makes. So read for structure, and pay attention to the direction of the objection, because several choices describe real argumentative techniques that simply are not this one.

The definition under attack says intelligence is the ability to figure out how things work in order to overcome obstacles. That final clause is the target. The author then builds a hypothetical case: suppose we became convinced some being understood how things work, and suppose we were also sure that understanding was not prompted by any specific obstacle. His claim is that we would still credit that being with intelligence. From there he concludes the definition is inadequate.

Name the shape of that move. He imagines applying the definition to a case, finds that it delivers a verdict our settled judgment rejects, and treats that clash as disqualifying. The definition is too narrow - it withholds the label from something we would not hesitate to call intelligent. Expect an answer about a hypothetical case producing counterintuitive results, and be ready to reject any choice that reverses the direction and complains the definition is too broad.
explanation_A: Impracticality is a different objection altogether. This choice has the author saying the definition's terms make it hard to tell which cases fall under it. But he has no trouble applying it - he applies it cleanly to his imagined being and gets a definite answer. His complaint is that the answer is wrong, not that no answer is forthcoming.
explanation_B: Correct. Each element matches. The author constructs a hypothetical - a being we become convinced understands how things work, with no obstacle prompting that understanding. He applies the psychologist's definition to it, which withholds intelligence because the obstacle-driven clause goes unsatisfied. Then he appeals to our intuition: we would certainly not deny this being intelligence. The definition therefore yields a verdict we would not accept, and that unacceptable consequence is the whole ground for calling it inadequate.
explanation_C: This gets the direction backwards. Saying a definition is not narrow enough is saying it lets in too much. The author's grievance is the reverse: the obstacle clause makes the definition too restrictive, excluding a being he thinks plainly counts as intelligent. The tail of the choice, about the definition being applicable, repeats the practicality complaint that is also absent here.
explanation_D: The most attractive wrong answer, because it correctly identifies the author as rejecting a definition on the strength of a case. Then check which way the case cuts. This choice describes overinclusion - the term applying to things it normally does not. The author's hypothetical being is the opposite: something the definition refuses to cover that we would normally cover. One word, "apply," where you need "fail to apply," turns a correct structure into the wrong one.
explanation_E: No appeal to authority is diagnosed anywhere. The author mentions that a cognitive psychologist advanced the definition, but he never suggests anyone accepts it because a psychologist said so, and he does not attack the source. His argument runs entirely on the content of the definition and what it implies about his imagined case.

Explanation:
This is a principle-justify question, which behaves like a sufficient assumption task. The correct principle, added to the premises, should make the conclusion follow. So isolate what the premises establish and what the conclusion demands, then find the rule that carries you from one to the other.

The premises say that genetically engineered crops are being adopted fast and monitored loosely, which creates a significant risk of damage to sensitive ecosystems, and they offer an illustration: one such crop was already in wide use when a study found it could threaten monarch butterflies. The conclusion is a requirement with a timing element - rigorous safety testing should be required before any new genetically engineered crop enters agricultural production.

Notice the gap. The premises give you potential environmental risk; the conclusion demands prior testing. What you need is a rule connecting those two: if something might harm the environment, it should not enter production until its safety has been tested. Prephrase that before reading on. Any principle that instead tells you what to do after testing results arrive, or when testing may be skipped, leaves the conclusion's requirement unestablished.
explanation_A: This rule bars production when testing has already shown a crop to be risky. It presupposes the testing has happened, which is precisely what the environmentalist wants mandated. Adding it changes nothing: a crop that was never tested would still be free to enter production, because the rule's trigger never fires. A principle about what test results obligate cannot establish an obligation to test.
explanation_B: Read the condition carefully - it covers crops with no potential for environmental risk and permits those to skip testing. That is the wrong half of the conditional. It tells you when testing is unnecessary, not when it is required, and you can accept it wholeheartedly while still allowing untested risky crops into production. Students pick this because it mentions risk and testing in the right vocabulary; the logical direction is inverted.
explanation_C: Correct, and it closes the gap exactly. The rule bars any crop that might present environmental risks from entering agricultural production unless its safety has been thoroughly tested. The premises already supply the trigger: genetically engineered crops pose a significant risk to sensitive ecosystems, and the monarch example shows the risk is real rather than theoretical. Apply the rule and the requirement in the conclusion follows - testing first, production after. Note also that the rule's "unless" places the testing before admission, matching the conclusion's timing rather than merely regulating crops already in the fields.
explanation_D: The timing is wrong. This principle governs crops that are already in agricultural production and says to discontinue them if testing reveals risk. The environmentalist's conclusion is about the gate, not the exit - what must happen before a new crop is planted. The monarch case actually illustrates why after-the-fact remedies are the problem, so this rule addresses the failure the argument is trying to prevent.
explanation_E: This tells you when further testing may stop: once rigorous studies find no evidence of risk. Like the other near-misses, it operates downstream of testing that has already occurred and so cannot generate the duty to test in the first place. It also runs mildly against the argument's spirit, since the monarch study shows risks can surface late.

Explanation:
This is a flaw question, so the right answer names a specific defect in the faculty member's reasoning - not a defect in the president's. Keep the two arguments separate, because the trap answers describe errors the president makes or errors nobody makes.

Track the structure. The president's argument runs: a university is a business, students are consumers, businesses must satisfy consumer demand, so programs that do not serve student demand should go. The faculty member's response consists of one objection - education is not analogous to providing consumer goods - and then a conclusion: the president is mistaken in claiming that programs should be tailored to student demand.

Look at what that objection can and cannot buy. Breaking the analogy shows the president's support is no good; it does not show his position is false. Programs might still deserve tailoring to student demand for reasons having nothing to do with commerce. Prephrase the flaw as: treating a bad argument for a claim as proof that the claim itself is wrong. That is a standard pattern worth memorizing, and it is the move the faculty member makes in a single step.
explanation_A: This describes a failure to engage with opposing argument, which is the opposite of what happens. The faculty member does nothing but engage with the president's argument - rebutting the business analogy is the entirety of the response. The real problem is that having dispatched the argument, the faculty member treats the view itself as refuted.
explanation_B: Popular opinion plays no part here. No one's reasoning rests on what most people believe; the faculty member's single piece of support is a claim about disanalogy between education and consumer goods. Note that student demand is the subject matter under discussion, not evidence anyone appeals to - that surface resemblance is what makes this choice look relevant.
explanation_C: Attractive because the argument is visibly about an analogy. But assign the error to the right party. Treating merely analogous things as identical is roughly what the faculty member accuses the president of doing in equating a university with a business. The faculty member's own move is to deny the analogy, which is not this flaw at all. Watch for choices that correctly describe the reasoning being criticized rather than the reasoning doing the criticizing.
explanation_D: Calling the president "financially minded" is a characterization, but the rejection does not rest on it. The faculty member's stated ground is the disanalogy between education and consumer goods, and the conclusion would be reached in exactly the same way with that phrase deleted. A personal-attack answer needs the attack to be doing the argumentative work; here it is scene-setting.
explanation_E: Correct. The faculty member shows only that the president's reason - the business-and-consumer analogy - fails to support his position. From that, the conclusion leaps to the president being mistaken in his claim. But an unsupported view is not thereby a false one; other considerations could still justify tailoring programs to student demand, and the faculty member never rules them out. Rejecting a view because someone argued badly for it is exactly the defect described.

Explanation:
This is a strengthen question, so the correct answer makes the conclusion more likely without having to prove it. It typically does this by shoring up the assumption the argument leans on hardest.

The evidence is a pattern: five East African groups belong to one subspecies, two West African groups to another, and one of the East African groups turned out behaviorally closer to the West African groups than to its own genetic relatives. The conclusion is causal - these grooming and foraging behaviors are determined by cultural factors rather than genetics. The evidence does real work against genetics, since a genetic account predicts that behavior tracks subspecies and this one group breaks that line. But notice what it does not do: showing genetics fails does not by itself show culture succeeded. Culture is one alternative among several, and the argument simply assumes it is the operative one.

So prephrase a strengthener that makes cultural transmission a live mechanism among chimpanzees - something establishing that behaviors can in fact pass between chimps along non-genetic lines. That converts culture from an unsupported label into a plausible explanation of the odd group.
explanation_A: Correct, and it supplies precisely the missing mechanism. The study's anomaly - one East African group behaving like the West African groups - needs an explanation that does not run through shared ancestry. If chimpanzees copy one another's behavior regardless of genetic closeness, then behaviors can spread along social rather than hereditary routes, which is what "cultural" means in this argument. That makes imitation a real pathway by which the odd group could have acquired grooming and foraging patterns matching a different subspecies, so the conclusion stops being a bare assertion and becomes the natural reading of the data.
explanation_B: This looks helpful at first because immigration into a group suggests transmitted behavior. Read the second half, though: newcomers bring new genetic characteristics along with the new behaviors. That hands the genetic explanation a route to the same anomaly - the deviant East African group might carry genes from elsewhere. Rather than favoring culture over genetics, the choice keeps the rival alive.
explanation_C: Different environmental challenges at different locations introduces a third explanation, environment, which competes with culture just as genetics does. Worse for the argument, environment is tied to location, so it would predict the East African groups resembling each other - the opposite of the finding the author is trying to explain. This leaves the conclusion weaker, not stronger.
explanation_D: True of the study, perhaps, but inert. Saying the behavioral differences are large enough to tell every group apart describes the data's granularity; it says nothing about what produced those differences. Both a genetic account and a cultural account are perfectly compatible with groups being distinguishable, so the choice cannot push you toward either.
explanation_E: Proximity is the tempting hook, since cultural transmission plausibly travels between neighbors. Follow it through, though. If the five East African groups live closer together than the two West African groups do, a proximity-driven cultural account predicts the East African groups converging on one another - exactly the pattern the study did not find. The choice makes the anomalous group harder to explain culturally.

Explanation:
This is a necessary assumption question. The correct answer is something the argument cannot do without, so the test is negation: deny the choice, and the argument should collapse. Beware of choices that would help the essayist but are stronger than the argument needs - necessary assumptions are usually modest.

The conclusion is narrow. The essayist does not say current testing procedures are wrong; he says it would be wrong to defend them simply by pointing out that subjects are volunteers who are informed of the risks and paid for them. The support is a contrast: paying people for what they freely choose is fine, but the same cannot be said when the choice is made under duress.

Now find the hinge. That contrast only undercuts the defense if the facts cited - being apprised of the risks, being compensated, being called a volunteer - leave open the possibility that the choice was not free. If being informed guaranteed freedom, the defense would go through untouched and the essayist would have no argument. So prephrase: knowing the risks does not settle whether the choice was free. That is the gap the essayist silently relies on.
explanation_A: Correct, and the negation test shows why it is required. Suppose possessing information about the consequences of one's choices did ensure those choices were free. Then the test subjects, having been apprised of the risks, chose freely; by the essayist's own concession it is not wrong to pay people for freely chosen acts; and the appeal to informed, compensated volunteers would be a perfectly good defense. The conclusion would be false. The argument therefore needs exactly this: information about risks does not by itself establish that a choice was free, which is what leaves room for the duress worry to apply.
explanation_B: Far stronger than anything the essayist needs, and in tension with what he grants. He explicitly allows that paying people for what they freely choose is not wrong, so he is not committed to the sweeping claim that voluntariness never justifies a transaction. His objection is only that these particular facts fail to establish genuine voluntariness in the first place.
explanation_C: This equates every shortfall in freedom with externally imposed duress. The essayist needs no such universal claim; it is enough that the cited facts leave the possibility of duress open. Negate this choice - allow that some unfree acts involve no external duress - and the argument runs exactly as before, since the essayist's point survives as long as duress remains one live possibility among others.
explanation_D: Tempting, because the essayist does seem to concede something in this neighborhood when he says paying people for freely chosen acts is not wrong. The difference is the condition. His concession is hedged on free choice; this choice strips that condition out and blesses accepting money for risk unconditionally. An assumption the argument would be embarrassed by is not an assumption it requires.
explanation_E: A broad permission principle about action, reaching well past anything in the argument. The essayist is evaluating whether a particular defense of testing procedures works, not laying down what people should be permitted to do. Deny this choice entirely and his reasoning is undisturbed, which is the clearest sign it is not necessary.

Explanation:
This is a must-be-true question. The correct answer has to be guaranteed by the statements given - not likely, not sensible, but inescapable. With conditional material like this, the answer is very often a contrapositive, so translate before you read the choices.

The first sentence is the conditional one: if a maple is healthy and has a trunk 12 or more inches in diameter, then tapping it will not harm it. Two conditions on the left, one result on the right. The remaining sentences are a different matter entirely - silver, red, and Manitoba maples can be tapped, and sugar maples are best for syrup because their sap has the highest sugar concentration. Those add species facts and a quality ranking; they say nothing about harm.

Take the contrapositive of the first sentence. If tapping does harm a tree, then it is not the case that the tree was both healthy and 12 inches or more across - so a harmed tree of sufficient diameter must have been unhealthy. Prephrase that. Then watch for the classic trap of negating both conditions and expecting the opposite result, and for answers that convert "best for syrup" into "most commonly used."
explanation_A: Correct, and it is the contrapositive stated in plain language. The rule says healthy plus a trunk of 12 inches or more guarantees no harm from tapping. So if a maple with a trunk over 12 inches is harmed by tapping, the guarantee did not hold, which means one of its conditions must have failed. The diameter condition is satisfied by assumption, since a trunk more than 12 inches across is also 12 or more. That leaves only one possibility: the tree was not healthy. The inference is airtight.
explanation_B: This asserts a correlation between health and trunk size. The stimulus mentions both properties, but only as two separate requirements that happen to appear in the same conditional. Nothing there links them to each other - a small tree may be perfectly healthy and a large one diseased. Co-occurrence in a rule is not evidence of association in the world.
explanation_C: Here the claim concerns what happens after a tree is harmed. The stimulus only tells you when harm will not occur; it never describes harm's consequences, and sap yield is never mentioned at all. The sap discussion that does appear is about sugar concentration across species, which is a different property entirely.
explanation_D: The classic trap, and worth slowing down for. It takes the original rule and negates both conditions - unhealthy instead of healthy, under 12 inches instead of 12 or more - then flips the result to harm. But a conditional tells you nothing about cases where its trigger fails. Knowing that healthy large maples are safe leaves the fate of unhealthy small ones completely open; they might be harmed, they might not.
explanation_E: Attractive because the stimulus does single out the sugar maple. Notice the exact claim, though: sugar maples are best for syrup making, on account of sugar concentration. Being best is a statement about quality; being most commonly used is a statement about practice. Availability, cost, or regional distribution could easily make some other maple the one syrup makers actually tap most often.

Explanation:
This is a flaw question, so the correct answer has to describe something the spokesperson's reasoning actually does wrong, not merely a claim you could quarrel with.

The conclusion is that the company's products are the best available, despite being the priciest. The support is a conditional about competitors: take any cheaper rival product, and if it were as good as or better than this company's, it would cost at least as much. Notice what that conditional assumes. It holds only if price reliably tracks quality in this industry, so that nothing can match these products without matching their price. But that is just another way of saying the most expensive products are the best ones, which is the very thing being argued for.

Before you look at the choices, expect something about circularity: the premise cannot be accepted by anyone who does not already accept the conclusion.
explanation_A: Correct. The spokesperson's one piece of support is the claim that any cheaper competing product would cost as much as this company's products if it were as good. Accepting that requires you to believe quality and price move together here, which is exactly the conclusion that these top-priced products are the best available. The premise therefore smuggles in what it is supposed to establish, and the argument runs in a circle.
explanation_B: The distinction drawn here is between what is best among existing products and what is best among producible ones. The spokesperson only ever claims superiority over products competitors actually make, and the conclusion is explicitly about what is available, so no such distinction is needed. Nothing in the argument slides from one sense of best to the other.
explanation_C: This points to a cause-and-effect reversal. Tempting, since price and quality are both in play, but trace the direction the spokesperson actually argues: the conditional runs from a product being as good to its costing as much, and that direction is never flipped. The reasoning reaches its verdict on quality by contraposing that conditional, not by treating an effect of high price as its cause. The defect is that the conditional itself is unearned, not that it inverts anything.
explanation_D: Composition flaws move from parts to whole, and this choice describes one: attributing to the company what holds of each product. Look at what is concluded, though. The spokesperson's conclusion is about the products themselves being the best available, not about the firm possessing some property. No aggregation step appears anywhere in the argument.
explanation_E: Inconsistency would mean the spokesperson asserts things that cannot both be true. Test them: the products are the most expensive, they are the best, and any cheaper rival that matched them would cost as much. Those fit together comfortably, indeed a little too comfortably, since the third is doing the work of guaranteeing the second. The problem is redundancy, not contradiction.

Explanation:
This is a principle-justify question. The correct principle has to bridge the argument's premises to its conclusion, making the inference go through rather than merely sounding agreeable.

The conclusion is a legal one: patenting an organism's genes should be illegal. Two reasons are offered. The first is that a person should not count as the inventor of something merely discovered, and genes, the argument takes for granted, are discovered rather than invented. The second, that profiting from genetic information is selfish and irresponsible, is moral colour; it never touches patent law. So the gap sits between not being an inventor and not being allowed to patent. The argument simply assumes that patents belong to inventors and to no one else.

Expect a principle that denies discoverers any patent entitlement.
explanation_A: What this offers is a label for people who profit from genetic information. The argument already asserts that such exploitation is selfish, so the principle restates a premise instead of connecting it to anything. Even granting that these people are selfish, nothing follows about what the law should permit, and the conclusion is about legality.
explanation_B: Correct. The argument establishes only that someone who discovers a gene is not its inventor, then jumps straight to a ban on patenting. This principle supplies precisely the missing link: discovery confers no entitlement to a patent. Apply it to a gene, which the argument treats as discovered, and the right to patent it disappears, which is what the conclusion needs. Notice that the principle does this work alone; the remark about selfishness contributes nothing to it.
explanation_C: Read the qualifier. Saying that discovery does not always amount to invention is weaker than the argument's own premise, which flatly denies that a discoverer is an inventor. More importantly, it still says nothing about patents. You could accept it entirely and have no reason at all to make gene patents illegal.
explanation_D: Here the restriction falls on profiting from another person's invention. That is the wrong party and the wrong relationship: the argument's complaint is that genes are nobody's invention, not that one person is cashing in on someone else's work. Applied to genes, this principle never triggers, since there is no original inventor being unfairly bypassed.
explanation_E: This grants inventors a patent entitlement, which is the converse of what the argument needs. Knowing that inventors may patent tells you nothing about whether non-inventors may; reading it as a prohibition on everyone else confuses a sufficient condition for patenting with a necessary one. The choice attracts because it puts inventors and patents in one sentence, but it points the conditional the wrong way.

Explanation:
The stem asks you to identify a possibility the premises leave open that would make the conclusion false, which is a way of asking you to name the logical gap.

Set out the pieces. The conditional premise covers O'Brien's students: any of them who heard the lecture from the beginning would have found it fascinating. The factual premise reports that some of his students did find it fascinating. The conclusion is that some of them must therefore have heard it from the beginning. That reverses the conditional. Hearing the lecture from the start is sufficient for a student's being fascinated, not necessary for it, so a student could have arrived late and still been captivated.

Expect the credited answer to describe a world in which the fascinated students are precisely the ones who did not hear the opening.
explanation_A: Students who were interested in Mercado's work but could not attend fall outside the argument's reach. Their existence is compatible with the conclusion as well as with the premises, since other students could still have arrived on time and been fascinated. A possibility that leaves the conclusion standing cannot be the reason it fails to follow.
explanation_B: The people described here are not O'Brien's students, and the conditional premise is explicitly limited to his students. Whatever non-students thought of the lecture, early arrival or not, has no bearing on whether some of his own students heard the opening. This is out of scope by the premise's own wording.
explanation_C: This one feels close, because latecomers are the right idea. But it describes students who were late and unfascinated, which tells you nothing about the fascinated students the second premise guarantees. Those students still need accounting for, and for all this choice says, they were fascinated because they heard the lecture from the start. The conclusion survives untouched.
explanation_D: Correct. Suppose no one who both heard the lecture from the beginning and found it fascinating was a student of O'Brien's. Then none of his fascinated students heard the opening, and in fact no student of his heard the opening at all, since the first premise guarantees that any who did would have been fascinated and so would belong to the excluded group. Both premises survive intact while the conclusion fails, which is exactly what exposes the reversed conditional.
explanation_E: Notice the shift in what is being heard. The argument's condition is hearing the lecture from the beginning; this choice concerns failing to hear the entire lecture despite arriving on time. Someone can hear the opening, miss a disrupted middle, and still satisfy the premise. Missing later portions never bears on whether a student heard the start.

Explanation:
A must-be-true question gives you facts rather than an argument, so the correct answer is whatever the statements force. Anything that needs an extra assumption is out.

There are two pieces. First, a split among moral virtues according to their effect on the person who has them: honesty tends to benefit its possessor, generosity tends not to. Second, a rule about effects on other people: a characteristic that tends to be detrimental to others is not a moral virtue. Take the contrapositive of that rule, that every moral virtue tends not to be detrimental to others, and then notice that the first sentence has already handed you two characteristics labelled moral virtues.

Before reading the choices, expect a modest claim about honesty or generosity not harming other people.
explanation_A: The claim here concerns a person with no moral virtues at all and what their characteristics do for others. The statements only tell you which characteristics fail to qualify as virtues; they never say that non-virtues are unhelpful. A thoroughly unvirtuous person might have traits that benefit others enormously, and nothing in the material rules that out.
explanation_B: Correct. Honesty is offered in the first sentence as an example of a moral virtue. The second sentence rules that anything tending to be detrimental to other people is not a moral virtue; contraposed, every moral virtue tends not to be detrimental to others. Run honesty through that and the result follows with no further assumption. Note how little is being claimed, too: not that honesty helps other people, only that it does not tend to harm them.
explanation_C: This is a comparison between virtuous and non-virtuous people in terms of benefit to others. Two problems. The rule speaks of not being detrimental, which is well short of being beneficial, and the statements make no comparative claim about people at all. Absence of harm does not add up to greater benefit than someone else provides.
explanation_D: Watch the first half carefully. The stimulus says generosity tends not to benefit the person who has it; this choice converts that into generosity being to one's own detriment. Failing to benefit someone and harming them are different things, and the gap between them is where this answer dies. The second half, about not harming others, does follow, but a choice earns the credit only if all of it is supported.
explanation_E: Here the conditional runs backwards. The rule given is that a moral virtue is never detrimental to others; this choice makes benefiting others enough to qualify a characteristic as a moral virtue. That reverses the relationship and upgrades not detrimental into beneficial at the same time. Some trait might benefit people without being any kind of virtue, and nothing in the statements excludes it.

Explanation:
This is a parallel reasoning question, so you are matching the shape of the argument, not its subject. Build an abstract template from the original and test the choices against it.

The original reports an observed result from a past period: during last year's flu season, nobody who was vaccinated caught the flu. It then notes that a group has been vaccinated now, namely every student at South High. From this it predicts that during this flu season none of those students will catch the flu. The move that matters is temporal. What held of vaccination last season is projected onto a different season, as though one year's perfect record were a standing rule.

So expect a choice with the same three beats: an observation confined to a past period, a present application of the same measure, and a prediction about the period ahead.
explanation_A: Correct. The beats line up exactly. Last month's observation plays the role of last flu season's: no camper who used repellent was bothered by mosquitoes. Tonight's application of repellent by everyone in the campsite matches this year's vaccination of every South High student. And the conclusion predicts a coming period's outcome, that nobody will be disturbed tonight, just as the original predicts this season's. The same unwarranted projection of one period's record onto another drives both.
explanation_B: Only one subject appears here, Marie's car, so there is no group to generalise over, and the past fact concerns how the car was maintained rather than an outcome observed across many cases. The conclusion is hedged with unlikely, while the original flatly claims that none will contract the flu. Both the structure and the force of the conclusion are off.
explanation_C: This is the trap. Every piece looks right, a rule from last year, a group that satisfies it, a conclusion drawn, but check the time frames. The students with perfect attendance and the advanced history class both belong to last year, and so does the conclusion. The reasoning stays inside a single period, which makes it valid, whereas the original's whole problem is the leap from one period to the next.
explanation_D: What this argument does is conclude something about everything in the refrigerator from facts about the fruit that was purchased. That error is about an unexamined possibility, namely other fruit also sitting in there, rather than about projecting a past period's outcome forward. There is no time shift and no prediction, so the template does not fit.
explanation_E: Here the first premise is a timeless generalisation about sparrows, not an observation confined to a past stretch of time. Combined with a fact about this tree's seeds, it yields its conclusion by straightforward application, and the reasoning is valid. The original depends on a premise true of one season being carried into another, which has no counterpart in this choice.

Explanation:
This is a complete-the-argument question, which functions as an inference task: the blank is the conclusion, and the right choice is the one the preceding sentences actually establish.

Start with the author's target. Advertising agencies are said to be wrongly blamed for making people want things they do not need. The explanation offered is that purchases are driven mainly by a belief that the product will satisfy desires the buyer already has, and the author concedes that producing that belief is precisely what agencies set out to do. So the sentences divide the work in two: the desire is the buyer's and already in place, while the belief that this product will satisfy it is the agency's contribution.

The blank completes a sentence about those desires, so expect it to say that advertisers work on desires already present rather than manufacturing them.
explanation_A: Reclassifying desires as needs would hand the critics their point back. The author's defence is not that people really need what they buy; it is that the desires predate the advertising. Nothing in the stimulus offers any test for what counts as a need either, so defining needs by whether a purchase follows comes from outside the argument entirely.
explanation_B: Two things go wrong. The stimulus never sorts advertising claims into true and false ones, so that distinction is imported. And the author's position is that advertisers do not create these desires at all, whereas this choice concedes that false advertising does create them, giving away the very charge the argument sets out to rebut.
explanation_C: Whether purchases actually deliver satisfaction is a question the stimulus never raises. Everything said concerns what buyers believe before purchasing and who is responsible for that belief. A claim about products routinely disappointing people would also sit oddly as the conclusion of a passage defending advertising agencies.
explanation_D: Correct. The defence of advertisers rests on separating two things: the desire a buyer brings to the purchase and the belief that a particular product will satisfy it. The author grants that agencies induce the belief, which is how they turn an existing desire to commercial use, and insists the desire itself is not their doing, since otherwise the criticism in the first sentence would stand. Exploited rather than created names exactly that division, and the sentence being completed is about those desires.
explanation_E: Look at the direction of influence. The stimulus has advertising inducing a belief about what a product will do; this choice makes the desires themselves the thing that gets people to believe advertisers. That turns the causal arrow around, and the author never addresses why consumers find advertising claims credible in the first place.

Explanation:
This is a parallel-flaw question, so you need the pattern of the error, not just a matching topic or a similarly odd conclusion.

Lay out the artist's reasoning. The evidence is a run of cases in which good work went unrewarded: the artist's own widely recognised paintings never won, and six other popular artists did no better. The conclusion is that winning the competition proves an artist is no good. Two things go wrong at once. The argument flips a claim about losers being good into a claim about winners being bad, which does not follow, and it reaches a universal verdict about every winner from a handful of unsuccessful entrants, none of whom are winners at all.

Before comparing choices, fix the template: good performers consistently fail to be rewarded, therefore being rewarded proves you are bad.
explanation_A: The researcher starts from the same materials, unrewarded inventions that are patented and lucrative, with other scientists reporting the same. But look where it lands: the judges must be using some criterion other than marketability. That is a cautious conclusion about the judging process, and it stays within what the evidence could suggest. The artist's conclusion condemns the winners themselves, and that is the move a parallel answer has to reproduce.
explanation_B: Attractive, because the conclusion has the same provocative shape. The difference lies in the evidence. The cook's cases are all winners whose food the public dislikes, so the argument generalises from winners to winners. The artist argues from people who never won and must therefore flip from what losing shows to what winning proves. Without that flip, the pattern of error is not the same one.
explanation_C: The professor's evidence is that identical essays fared differently in different years, and the conclusion is only that quality is not the sole criterion. That is a reasonable inference from the inconsistency, and it passes no judgement on the winners. Neither the flip nor the sweeping verdict found in the artist's argument shows up here.
explanation_D: Correct. The student's proposals carry broad support yet are never taken seriously, and other people's widely supported proposals are ignored too, so good work goes unrewarded across several cases. From that the student concludes that the student government takes only bad proposals seriously, a verdict about the proposals that do get attention. The same flip from rejected-but-good to accepted-therefore-bad appears, resting on a sample that contains no accepted proposals at all.
explanation_E: What the travel agent concludes is about the airlines' intentions, that they want to discourage good ideas and hard work. Reasoning from a pattern of rewards to the motive behind them is a different error from inferring the quality of the winners. The evidence also comes from one person's experience, with nothing matching the other entrants the artist brings in.

explanation_A: Legacy and influence would require the passage to trace what came after Ormes: cartoonists she inspired, later strips that borrowed from her, a reputation that grew or faded. None of that appears. The discussion stays inside the thirteen months of the strip itself, analysing its content and its cultural work. Describing Ormes as little-known is also unsupported, since the passage notes her own success as a cartoonist. A choice can name the right subject and still fail by naming the wrong activity, which is exactly what happens here.
explanation_B: This phrasing is lifted almost intact from a single sentence near the end of the third paragraph, which is what makes it tempting. But leaving a record of a moment in jazz is one consequence the passage mentions in passing, not the project it undertakes. Nothing in the first, second or fourth paragraphs falls under it: the authorship claim, the fairy-tale framing and the segregation material are all left outside. Watch for choices that take a true subordinate detail and promote it to thesis.
explanation_C: The parallel between improvisation in swing and tap dance and the form of the strip is real, but notice who draws it. Ormes does, inside several episodes; the passage reports that she did so rather than conducting a technical comparison of cartooning and jazz on its own account. Even granting that it did, the comparison occupies one sentence of the third paragraph and nothing else. Two defects stack here, wrong scale and wrong party, and either alone is enough.
explanation_D: The fairy-tale resemblance is laid out in the second paragraph, so a student who weights that section heavily will find this plausible. The third paragraph then opens by conceding the fantastic gestures only to argue past them, which makes the resemblance a foil rather than a conclusion. Selecting this reverses the passage: it treats the position the author complicates as the position the author defends. Ask what the passage does after the comparison and the choice dissolves.
