The argument jumped from the crab not being bioluminescent itself straight to the crab hunting bioluminescent prey, and this choice shows the identical facts fitting a defensive purpose just as comfortably. With a rival explanation of the receptors available, hunting is no longer the probable account, and the conclusion loses its footing.

Explanation:
This is a resolve-the-discrepancy question. The correct answer must make both halves of a surprising pair fit together, and here it has to explain not merely why the faulty commercials failed to hurt sales but why they did better than the competition's.

Lay out the two facts. One agency produced commercials in which sound and picture were out of sync, obviously so during dialogue, and viewers complained. Yet the car dealerships using that agency saw bigger sales increases than dealerships whose commercials came from elsewhere. Read the comparison carefully: both groups advertised on television, so anything affecting television advertising across the board cannot open a gap between them.

A prephrase: the defect must have carried some unintended benefit. Look for the choice that turns the annoyance into an advantage, most naturally that a jarring commercial lodges in the memory, and a remembered dealership is one a viewer eventually drives to.
explanation_A: Muting the sound would hide the synchronization problem, but hiding a handicap is not the same as producing an advantage. Worse, the choice says viewers silenced local dealership commercials generally, which would strike the other agencies' spots just as hard. What needs explaining is a gap between two groups, and nothing here opens one.
explanation_B: Correct. Advertising works through recall, so if poor synchronization makes a commercial more memorable, the dealerships stuck with the defective spots were handed better name recognition than their rivals. That maps exactly onto the comparison in the stimulus: this agency's clients had the flawed commercials, the other dealerships did not, and the flawed ones stayed in viewers' heads. The complaints and the extra sales then coexist without contradiction, because being irritating and being remembered are not opposites.
explanation_C: True or not, this reports who the studio's clients happened to be, not what effect its commercials had. Knowing that most of its advertisers were car dealerships tells you nothing about why those dealerships outperformed dealerships advertising through other agencies, and that performance gap is the only thing in need of explanation.
explanation_D: This chips away at the size of the problem by noting that some spots had no talking heads, and students pick it for exactly that reason. A smaller defect is still a defect, though, and the dealerships at other agencies had no synchronization problem at all. Shrinking a disadvantage cannot account for a sales increase that outran everyone else's.
explanation_E: Dealerships that barely used television fall outside the comparison entirely. The stimulus contrasts dealerships relying on this agency's commercials with dealerships relying on other agencies' commercials; a third group doing little television advertising has no bearing on the difference between the first two.

Explanation:
This is a role-of-a-claim question. To answer it you must map the argument's structure first and only then ask where the specified statement sits in that structure: what supports it, and what it supports.

The passage makes three moves. Proponents report that sinking obsolete equipment in coral areas provides much-needed habitats, and from that they infer the practice is ecologically sound. The author pushes back, holding that the practice may be ecologically unsound even if it does provide those habitats. Then comes the word for, and after it the statement at issue, that the practice may upset an area's ecological balance in unknown ways.

For introduces support. The unknown-balance claim is the reason the author gives for thinking the practice could be unsound despite the habitat benefit, so it holds up the author's position rather than being held up by anything else. Expect the answer to call it a premise.
explanation_A: A summary restates an argument's overall point, but this claim is narrower than the author's position and arrives as a reason for it. Read the final sentence whole and the order is conclusion first, support second. The word for introduces grounds; it never heads a recap.
explanation_B: Nothing in the passage attacks this claim. The author asserts it, and asserts it approvingly. What the argument does resist is the proponents' move from habitats to ecological soundness, and confusing the thing being rebutted with the tool used to do the rebutting is precisely the error this choice invites.
explanation_C: Here is the trap, and it is a good one, because the description is accurate about the wrong claim. It is the habitat point that the author grants while denying it establishes ecological soundness. The unknown-balance claim is the author's own reason for that denial, not a claim whose sufficiency is under examination.
explanation_D: The main conclusion is the author's contrary position, that the practice may be ecologically unsound even while providing much-needed habitats. The specified claim is what the author offers in support of that position. Choosing this reverses the direction of support that the word for plainly establishes.
explanation_E: Correct. Follow the connective. The author states the conclusion, that the practice may be unsound even if it supplies habitats, and then writes for, signalling that what follows is the evidence. The possibility of upsetting an area's ecological balance in unknown ways is that evidence: it is the consideration meant to make the author's conclusion credible, which is what makes it a premise and nothing more.

Explanation:
This is a weaken question, so look for the choice that undercuts the link between the evidence and the conclusion rather than one that merely raises some other objection to the cameras.

The conclusion is that red-light cameras do not increase traffic safety, whatever they may do for municipal revenue. The support is a count: accidents go up at camera intersections, with side-impact collisions falling and rear-impact collisions rising significantly. The argument therefore equates safety with the raw number of collisions and treats the two crash types as interchangeable units.

That is the opening. Collisions are not equal in what they do to people, and the cameras are trading one kind for another. Before looking at the choices, expect something that separates the two types by severity, so that swapping side impacts for rear impacts could leave drivers safer even while the total climbs.
explanation_A: How a municipality spends its ticket revenue has no bearing on what happens at the intersections themselves. If anything this leans the author's way, reinforcing the suggestion that cameras are about money. Weakening requires attacking the inference from collision counts to safety, and spending priorities never reach it.
explanation_B: Undeserved tickets make cameras unfair, not ineffective. The conclusion is specifically about traffic safety, and a driver wrongly ticketed is still a driver who did not crash. Attacking a practice along some other dimension, in this case accuracy, is a standard distractor pattern in weaken questions.
explanation_C: Assigning fault for side-impact collisions to the driver who runs the red light connects cameras to the crashes they prevent, which is why this attracts attention. But blame is not harm. Knowing whose error causes side impacts tells you nothing about whether exchanging side impacts for rear impacts leaves road users better or worse off, which is the whole question.
explanation_D: Correct. The argument's entire weight rests on counting collisions, and this choice shows the count concealing what matters. If side impacts are a far greater safety threat than rear impacts, then cutting the dangerous type while adding the milder type can improve safety even though the total rises. The premise stays perfectly true and simply stops supporting the conclusion, which is exactly what a weakener should accomplish.
explanation_E: Ticketing the car's owner rather than its driver is a problem of accountability. It might even imply that cameras deter less effectively than they could, which helps the author rather than hurting. Either way it leaves untouched the inference from a higher collision total to no gain in safety.

Explanation:
This is a parallel-reasoning question with a twist in the stem: the correct choice must demonstrate the original's flaw by reproducing it in a form where the error is impossible to overlook. So diagnose the original first, then match the error rather than the subject matter.

Glenville once had the region's highest apartment rents and now ranks third. From that the argument concludes that renting there costs less than it used to. The mistake is treating a change in relative standing as a change in the underlying absolute figure. Glenville's rents could have climbed steadily while two other places climbed faster, and the ranking would still have slipped.

Prephrase the parallel before you read: something was ahead of a second thing, is now behind it, and the arguer concludes the first thing must have gone down, when the obvious explanation is that the second thing went up faster.
explanation_A: Only one comparison is made here, at a single moment, with no before-and-after ranking at all. The questionable step is treating veterinary spending as a measure of health. The original's error depends on two points in time and on reading an absolute decline out of a relative slide, so the shapes do not match.
explanation_B: Correct, and the parallel is exact. The kitten outranked the puppy in size, now ranks below it, and the arguer concludes the kitten must have shrunk, just as Glenville slipped from first to third and the arguer concluded rents must have fallen. In both cases the obvious alternative explanation is that the other party grew faster: the puppy has been growing, and other towns' rents have been rising. Casting the reasoning as a shrinking kitten makes the absurdity plain, which is precisely what the stem asks a demonstration to do.
explanation_C: Moving from birth order to order of acquisition is an inference from one fact to a loosely related one. Nothing in it involves rankings reversing or absolute quantities changing. Whatever is wrong with the reasoning, it does not reproduce the move from a fall in the standings to a decline in the thing itself.
explanation_D: Disqualify this one immediately: it is not clearly flawed, and a demonstration has to display the error. It compares two animals at a single moment and draws a modest prediction from the comparison, never claiming that a change in rank implies a change in any underlying amount.
explanation_E: The error here is assuming that a one-way change must be mutual, inferring the puppy's warmth from the kitten's. That is a reciprocity mistake rather than a confusion of relative position with absolute level, and there is no earlier ranking that has since reversed for the argument to misread.

Explanation:
This is an explain-the-discrepancy question, so the correct answer must supply a fact that makes the puzzling result unsurprising while leaving everything stated in the stimulus true.

Here is the puzzle. Crocodile attacks on humans at Lake Victoria have risen significantly over 20 years, yet the crocodile population has not grown and the crocodiles have no less food available than before. The stimulus has pre-emptively closed off the two obvious explanations, more crocodiles and hungrier crocodiles. Notice that it has closed off nothing at all on the human side of the encounter.

That is where your answer has to come from. The number of attacks depends not only on how many crocodiles there are and how well fed they are, but on how often people put themselves into crocodile habitat. Expect a choice establishing that humans now enter the lake, or more parts of the lake, far more than they once did.
explanation_A: Destroying crocodiles blamed for attacks would tend to push the attack rate down rather than up, and in any case the stimulus already reports that the population has not increased. A fact that works against the trend cannot be what explains it.
explanation_B: A head count of roughly 100 crocodiles in the high-attack area is a snapshot with no comparison to earlier decades. Explaining a change requires something that itself changed; a static figure, however precise, leaves the 20-year increase exactly as puzzling as it was before.
explanation_C: Comparing Lake Victoria with other parts of Africa answers a different question, namely where attacks are most common rather than why they have become more common here. Students reach for this because it sounds like confirmation that the lake has a crocodile problem, but a contrast across places cannot account for a trend across time.
explanation_D: Crocodiles unafraid of people and their boats helps explain why attacks happen at all, and nothing suggests this fearlessness is recent. What the stimulus asks you to account for is the rise. Unless the trait is new, it is a constant, and constants do not explain changes.
explanation_E: Correct. An attack requires a crocodile and a human to meet, and the stimulus rules out change only on the crocodile side: same numbers, same food supply. If people now fish across more of Lake Victoria than in previous decades, then humans are venturing into crocodile habitat in places and at rates they did not before, so the same crocodiles behaving the same way will run into far more people. More encounters produce more attacks, and the puzzle dissolves without contradicting anything given.

Explanation:
This is a strengthen question, so the correct answer does not have to prove the conclusion; it only has to make the conclusion more likely than it was before. The conclusion here is causal, and causal conclusions are strengthened in predictable ways: rule out a rival cause, or show that the effect behaves the way the proposed cause would make it behave.

Break the argument down. The premises are a correlation in time: clocks move forward, many people lose an hour of sleep, and the next day accidents run 7 percent above the seasonal average. The conclusion leaps from that timing to a cause, naming sleep deprivation as what is responsible. Notice everything else that also changes on that day. The clocks themselves changed, schedules shifted, light fell at different hours. Any of those could drive the spike, and the argument simply assumes sleep loss is the operative factor.

Before reading the choices, expect something that ties the accidents specifically to drowsiness rather than to the clock change in general. A finding that the extra accidents cluster at the hours when sleep-deprived people are most impaired is exactly that: the effect carries the fingerprint of the proposed cause.
explanation_A: Forgetting to change the clocks and running late is a competing explanation, not a supporting one. If people are having accidents because they are rushing to appointments they are late for, then something other than sleep deprivation is producing the spike. This choice points at a mechanism that operates on the same day and produces the same effect, which pulls support away from the author's causal claim rather than adding to it.
explanation_B: Seasonal accident rates are already neutralized by the way the statistic is reported. The 7 percent figure is a comparison against the average for that time of year, not against the annual average, so the fact that spring is generally safer than winter has already been factored out. The comparison baseline is doing the work this choice tries to supply, which leaves it with nothing to add.
explanation_C: Severity and incidence are different measurements, and the argument is about incidence. Whether the extra crashes are minor fender benders or serious collisions tells you nothing about what caused them to happen. You could imagine this cutting either way on a theory of drowsy driving, which is a sign it is simply not engaging with the inference the author drew.
explanation_D: Correct. This supplies the causal fingerprint the argument was missing. If sleep deprivation is driving the spike, the accidents should concentrate at the hours when sleep-deprived people are most impaired, and that is precisely the pattern reported here. A rival explanation like schedule confusion or a shifted commute would predict a spike at other hours instead. By matching the timing of the effect to the known timing of drowsiness, this choice makes sleep loss the best available account rather than merely one candidate among several.
explanation_E: Lingering effects would predict elevated accident rates across several days, but the statistic the author cites is confined to the single day after the change. Rather than reinforcing the inference, this invites the awkward question of why the spike is not spread out. At best it tells you something about sleep deprivation in general without connecting it to the specific one-day pattern the argument has to explain.

Explanation:
This question asks for the conclusion of the argument, so the correct answer is the single claim everything else is offered to support. Your job is not to find the most interesting or most general statement; it is to find the one that is being defended rather than doing the defending.

Work through the sentences by role. The opening sentence reports that every human brain contains a mental representation of the external world, which sets up the subject but is not in dispute. The second sentence begins with a contrastive signal and asserts that this representation necessarily leaves out much detail. Then comes the phrase that settles the structure: the material that follows is introduced as the reason to believe what just preceded it. What follows is a pair of supporting claims, that the external world is larger and more complex than the brain, and that nothing can completely represent something larger and more complex than itself.

Once you see that the last two claims are given as grounds, the conclusion has to be the claim they are grounds for. Treat the premise marker as a pointer aimed backward at the sentence it supports.
explanation_A: Correct. This is the claim introduced by the contrastive turn and then backed up by everything after it. The argument's support structure confirms it: the size and complexity comparison and the general impossibility claim are both offered as reasons, and the thing they are reasons for is that the brain's representation necessarily omits much detail. Strip away the supporting material and this is the sentence left standing on its own, which is the test for a conclusion.
explanation_B: The comparison of the external world to the brain in size and complexity arrives inside the supporting material, after the phrase that announces reasons are coming. It is one of the two facts marshalled to establish the omission of detail, so it is doing support work rather than receiving it. Students who are scanning for a sweeping-sounding statement can land here, but position within the support structure, not grandness, decides the issue.
explanation_C: This applies the general impossibility claim to the brain in particular, and it is the sort of thing the argument relies on along the way. But it is an intermediate step on the road to the conclusion, not the destination. The point the essay is driving at concerns what the brain's representation actually omits, and this choice stops short of saying anything about missing detail at all.
explanation_D: Here is the opening sentence, offered as uncontested background to establish that there is a representation to talk about in the first place. Nothing in the passage is presented as evidence for it. A conclusion is the claim under pressure, the one the author expects you to doubt until the reasons are supplied, and this claim is never put under any pressure.
explanation_E: This is the broad principle about representation that appears in the final clause, squarely inside the reasons the author gives. It is also stated in fully general terms covering any entity whatsoever, which is a hallmark of a premise being invoked rather than a conclusion being defended. The argument uses this principle; it does not argue for it.

Explanation:
This is a principle question running from the specific to the general: you are given a pair of statements and asked which broad principle they illustrate. The correct answer must be a general claim that the statements actually exemplify. Anything that goes beyond what the statements show, or that imports a recommendation they never make, fails even if it sounds reasonable.

The two statements are a general tendency and an exception to it. Generally, airing a false and harmful idea in open discussion reduces its appeal. But some misconceptions are alluring enough that debating them makes them more popular, and this happens even where democracy is thriving. Notice what the exception does to the comfortable assumption behind the general rule. The reason we value open discussion is the belief that exposure drives out error, and the second statement reports cases where exposure does the opposite.

Before looking at the choices, prephrase something like this: debate is not a reliable mechanism for advancing truth, because sometimes it spreads falsehood instead. Be strict about staying descriptive. The statements report what happens; they never say what anyone ought to do about it.
explanation_A: This jumps from a description to a policy, recommending that governments be permitted to suppress debate. Nothing in the statements endorses suppression, and the mention of a flourishing democracy is there to show the phenomenon is not a symptom of a defective society, not to invite censorship. Watch for answers that convert an observed drawback into a permission or a duty; the statements supply no normative premise at all.
explanation_B: Tempting, because it correctly registers that open discussion can boost a misconception, which is the exception the statements report. What kills it is the evaluative word better. Saying that discussion is sometimes the preferable course requires weighing costs against benefits, and the statements never make any such comparison. They tell you what discussion does, not whether doing it is worthwhile.
explanation_C: This asks you to carve the categories apart, claiming some pernicious ideas fall outside the class of misconceptions. The statements mention false and pernicious ideas in the general rule and misconceptions in the exception, but they never indicate how the two categories relate, and certainly never establish that one fails to contain the other. This is an inference about terminology that the material simply does not license.
explanation_D: Correct, and it is the principle the exception directly instantiates. The general rule rests on the hope that discussion drives out error. The second statement supplies cases where debating a misconception increases its popularity, which is error gaining ground through exactly the process that was supposed to defeat it. Generalize that and you get the claim that discussion and debate do not necessarily lead to wider acceptance of truth. Note how carefully hedged the wording is: not necessarily matches a stated exception to a general tendency, which is all the statements give you.
explanation_E: This proposes a causal account of the appeal, making falsity itself part of what attracts people. The statements say certain misconceptions happen to be alluring; they never explain why, and they never suggest the allure flows from being false. If anything the general rule points the other way, since it holds that exposing an idea as false usually reduces its appeal.

Explanation:
This is a flaw question aimed at one speaker in a dialogue, so the correct answer must describe something that goes wrong in Chandha's reply specifically. In a two-speaker flaw question the most common defect is a mismatch: the responder rebuts a claim the first speaker never made. Before diagnosing, pin down precisely what each person asserted.

Schmidt does not object to the township having maintenance rules. He objects to one method of enforcing them, namely encouraging residents to turn in their neighbors, and he gives two reasons: it sours relations between neighbors and it produces tips motivated by spite. His target is the enforcement mechanism, not the standards being enforced.

Chandha answers by defending the existence of the rules, pointing out that without them a single homeowner could spoil the look of a whole neighborhood. That may well be true, and Schmidt would likely grant it, because it addresses a position Schmidt never took. Expect the correct answer to say that Chandha has treated an objection to how the rules are enforced as though it were an objection to having the rules.
explanation_A: Correct. This names the substitution exactly. Schmidt's complaint is confined to a particular enforcement practice, soliciting reports from neighbors, and the harms he cites are harms of that practice. Chandha's reply never touches the practice; it argues that maintenance rules are needed at all. The defense would only answer Schmidt if his criticism had been aimed at the rules themselves, so Chandha has shifted the target. Notice that Schmidt could accept every word Chandha says and keep his objection intact, which is the clearest sign the reply misses the point.
explanation_B: Attacking motivation means impugning why the opponent argues as they do rather than engaging with the reasoning. Chandha says nothing about Schmidt's reasons for speaking, does not suggest bad faith, and makes no personal charge of any kind. Interestingly, it is Schmidt who raises the subject of spite, and he raises it about the people filing tips, not about anyone in the exchange.
explanation_C: This is the attractive wrong answer, because it is also a confusion-of-two-things description and it sits in the right neighborhood. Both halves miss, though. Schmidt is not criticizing the consequences of having rules, and Chandha is not defending any detailed provision. The real swap is between enforcement method and the rules' existence, and neither term in this choice captures the enforcement method. One wrong noun is enough to disqualify a flaw description.
explanation_D: The error described here is treating a likelihood as a certainty, sliding from often to always. Look for who might commit it. Schmidt says the practice engenders bad feelings and leads to spiteful tips, which is where any such overstatement would live. Chandha's reply contains no claim about frequency at all; it describes what could happen in the absence of rules, which is a possibility claim, not an inflated generalization.
explanation_E: This posits a muddle over the causal direction of bad feelings among neighbors, whether they are the cause or the result of something. Chandha never mentions bad feelings. The only speaker who brings them up is Schmidt, and he is clear that the reporting practice produces them. There is no causal confusion in the reply because there is no causal claim about neighborly relations in it.

Explanation:
This is a role of a claim question, so the correct answer must describe the function the specified statement performs in the argument, not whether it is true or how plausible it sounds. Map the argument's skeleton first and locate the claim within it.

The author is evaluating a criterion others have proposed: once we must think about computers in terms of beliefs and desires to understand how they work, we may rightly say they have beliefs and desires. The author then observes that we already need to think about what computers believe and desire, and draws out what the criterion therefore entails, that computers existing right now have beliefs and desires. The final sentence delivers the verdict: the criterion is obviously flawed.

That shape is a reductio. The author derives a consequence from someone else's standard and rejects the standard because the consequence is unacceptable. Crucially, the author does not endorse the claim about present-day computers. Its intolerability is the engine of the attack, and the word obviously signals that the author expects you to find it absurd on sight. So the claim functions as the unwelcome result that sinks the criterion.
explanation_A: Correct. The claim is what the criterion yields once you grant that we already need to interpret computers in terms of beliefs and desires, and the author treats that yield as intolerable. That is why the very next sentence condemns the criterion rather than accepting the result. The logic only works if the claim is unacceptable: a reductio refutes a standard by showing where it leads, so the derived consequence must be something the audience will refuse. This choice captures both halves, that the claim is a consequence of the criterion and that it is an unacceptable one.
explanation_B: Calling the claim an uncontroversial view gets the author's stance backwards. The author does not hold this view at all; it is attributed to the criterion as an implication and then used as grounds for rejecting it. There is a grain of truth buried here, in that the author expects agreement about how to react to the claim, but the agreement expected is that it is false, not that it is acceptable.
explanation_C: An example clarifying a criterion would illustrate how the standard works without bearing on whether it is correct. This claim does the opposite kind of work. It is derived from the criterion by applying it to the actual present situation, and it is deployed to discredit the criterion. A clarifying illustration leaves the standard standing; this claim is the reason the standard is declared flawed.
explanation_D: The conclusion is the final sentence, the judgment that the suggested criterion is obviously flawed. Everything before it, including the claim about present-day computers, is machinery for reaching that judgment. Students pick this because the claim is reached through an inference and sits near the end, but being the product of reasoning does not make a statement the main point when a further verdict follows from it.
explanation_E: Treating the claim as a premise whose truth the argument needs inverts its function. The argument succeeds only if the claim is false, or at least unacceptable, because its unacceptability is what condemns the criterion. If present-day computers really did have beliefs and desires, the criterion would have been vindicated rather than refuted. A statement the author needs you to reject cannot be a premise the author needs you to accept.

Explanation:
The phrase follows logically if which one of the following is assumed marks a sufficient assumption question. The correct answer must be strong enough that adding it to the premises makes the conclusion airtight. Diagram this one, because the trap choices differ from the answer only in the direction of the conditional.

The premise is a conditional: if the biggest competitor goes out of business, then some of the specialized suppliers both firms use would be bankrupted. The conclusion is also conditional, though the wording disguises it. Saying the competitor must stay in business in order for the manufacturer to stay in business means that the manufacturer staying in business requires the competitor staying in business, or equivalently, if the competitor goes under, the manufacturer goes under too.

Now see what is missing. The premise gets you from the competitor's failure to the suppliers' bankruptcy, and the conclusion needs to end at the manufacturer's failure. The unbridged span is between bankrupt suppliers and the manufacturer's survival. Prephrase it: if those suppliers are bankrupted, the manufacturer cannot stay in business. Equivalently, the manufacturer stays in business only if its specialized suppliers survive.
explanation_A: This makes a flat prediction that the suppliers will not be bankrupted rather than supplying a connection between supplier bankruptcy and the manufacturer's fate. The argument needs a link, not a forecast. Knowing how things will turn out for the suppliers leaves the conclusion's actual content, the dependence of the manufacturer's survival on the competitor's, without any grounding, because nothing here says what losing those suppliers would do to the manufacturer.
explanation_B: This says that the competitor staying in business is enough to keep the manufacturer afloat. The conclusion claims something quite different, that the competitor staying in business is required for it. Guaranteeing survival and being indispensable to survival are opposite relations, and this choice supplies the one the argument does not need. It would license concluding the manufacturer survives if the competitor does, never that it fails if the competitor fails.
explanation_C: Here the dependence runs the wrong way, making the competitor's fate hinge on the manufacturer's. The conclusion needs the manufacturer's survival to depend on the competitor's, which is the reverse. Added to the premises, this produces nothing: knowing what happens to the competitor when the manufacturer folds tells you nothing about what happens to the manufacturer when the competitor folds.
explanation_D: This is the choice that catches most students, because it involves exactly the right two things, supplier bankruptcy and the manufacturer staying in business, and differs from the credited answer by a single word. Read it precisely: if makes healthy suppliers sufficient for survival. The argument needs them to be necessary. Sufficiency lets you conclude the manufacturer survives when suppliers are fine; it never lets you conclude the manufacturer fails when they are not.
explanation_E: Correct, and the phrase only if is what makes it work. It establishes that surviving suppliers are a requirement for the manufacturer staying in business, so if those suppliers are bankrupted, the manufacturer cannot continue. Chain that onto the premise and the conclusion is forced: the competitor goes out of business, therefore some shared specialized suppliers are bankrupted, therefore the manufacturer cannot stay in business. Read the contrapositive back and you get precisely the stated conclusion, that the manufacturer's survival requires the competitor's.

Explanation:
This is a parallel reasoning question, so the correct answer must share the original's logical structure: the same quantifiers, the same arrangement of terms, and the same validity. Subject matter is irrelevant, and here every choice uses the same joggers-and-shoes material precisely so that only the structure can distinguish them. Abstract the original before you read any of them.

Three terms are in play: trains going by, howling, and washing the dog. The first premise is universal, since the dog howls whenever a train passes, so every train-passing is accompanied by a howl. The second premise is existential, since occasionally a train passes while Jack is washing the dog, so some train-passings overlap with washings. The conclusion is existential as well: some howling overlaps with washing.

In schematic form, all A are accompanied by B, some A coincide with C, therefore some B coincide with C. That reasoning is valid, and the universal first premise is what makes it so. Keep three things fixed as you test the choices: the first premise must be universal, the second must be existential, and the conclusion must be existential and must join the two non-shared terms in that order.
explanation_A: The pieces are all present but the second premise and the conclusion have traded places. This argument assumes that some people who can benefit from good shoes prefer sneakers and concludes that a few serious joggers prefer sneakers, which is the reverse of the original's movement. Running the inference backwards also makes it invalid, since the beneficiaries of good shoes may include many non-joggers. The original reasons soundly; a structural match must do the same.
explanation_B: Watch the first word. Most serious joggers is a majority claim, while the original's first premise is flatly universal, covering every train that goes by without exception. That downgrade breaks the parallel and also breaks the logic: the sneaker-preferring joggers could all come from the minority who would not benefit from good shoes. Swapping a universal for a mere majority is one of the most common structural mismatches on these questions.
explanation_C: Correct, and it matches on every axis. Any serious jogger can benefit from good running shoes is universal, exactly like the claim that the dog howls whenever a train goes by. A few serious joggers prefer ordinary sneakers is existential, mirroring the occasional train that passes during a washing. The conclusion then joins the two outer terms existentially, that some people who can benefit from good shoes prefer sneakers, just as some howling coincides with washing. The universal premise guarantees that every serious jogger belongs to the beneficiary group, so the few who prefer sneakers must sit in both categories. Same quantifiers, same order, and valid in the same way.
explanation_D: The opening premise is existential here, covering only at least some serious joggers, where the original's opening premise admits no exceptions. That single weakening is fatal to the parallel and to the reasoning, because the joggers who prefer sneakers might be drawn entirely from those who would not benefit. Two existential premises can never deliver a guaranteed conclusion, whereas the original's universal premise does exactly that.
explanation_E: The premises here are fine, pairing a universal with an existential as the original does, so the error is in the conclusion. It asserts that anyone who can benefit from good shoes occasionally prefers sneakers, a sweeping universal built on a premise about only some joggers. The original concludes modestly that the dog sometimes howls while being washed. Inflating an existential conclusion into a universal one is both a structural mismatch and an outright invalidity.

Explanation:
This is a most strongly supported question. There is no argument to critique, only a set of facts, and the correct answer is the claim those facts best underwrite. Be strict about the boundary between what the statements establish and what merely sounds consistent with them, because the wrong answers here all overshoot in a specific way.

Sort the information. First, a two-sided fact about plants: fast growth means they absorb more carbon dioxide than they release, while very slow growth reverses that balance. Then a conditional: any substantial increase in carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere raises temperatures in the tropics, which is where most of the world's plants live. Then a second conditional: the more tropical temperatures rise, the more slowly tropical plants grow on average.

The two conditionals chain. A substantial increase in released carbon dioxide produces higher tropical temperatures, and higher tropical temperatures produce slower average growth there. Note that the first conditional says nothing about where the carbon dioxide comes from, so the chain holds regardless of its source, including the plants themselves. Expect the answer to run that chain and stop there, without converting more slowly into very slowly or reversing either conditional.
explanation_A: This predicts an inevitable, steadily accelerating rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide, which is a runaway feedback loop the statements never close. To get acceleration you would need slower-growing plants to become net emitters, and that requires growth to become very slow, not merely slower. The word inevitably compounds the problem by ruling out every countervailing factor. The statements describe conditional tendencies, not an unstoppable trajectory.
explanation_B: This is the most tempting wrong answer, and a single modifier kills it. The statements say plants become net emitters only when growing very slowly, while the chain of conditionals delivers merely that tropical plants grow more slowly on average. Slower is not the same as very slow, so you cannot conclude the flip to net release has occurred. The choice also widens the subject from tropical plants to the bulk of Earth's plants, stretching beyond what the conditionals cover.
explanation_C: Correct, and it is just the chain of the two conditionals with the source of the carbon dioxide filled in. If tropical plants release enough carbon dioxide to raise the total released substantially, then by the first conditional tropical temperatures increase, and by the second, tropical plants grow more slowly on average. The first conditional is indifferent to where the gas originates, so plants supplying it changes nothing. Notice how carefully the wording is pitched: it claims only slower average growth, exactly what the second conditional delivers, and it stays inside the tropics, where both conditionals apply.
explanation_D: The direction of the reasoning is inverted here. The statements run from rising tropical temperatures to slower plant growth; this choice runs from slower growth back to a substantial temperature increase. Reversing a conditional is never licensed. The choice also skips two required steps, since slower growth alone does not make plants net emitters, and even net emission would have to be large enough to raise the total released substantially.
explanation_E: Another reversal, this time of the first conditional. The statements hold that a substantial increase in released carbon dioxide produces higher tropical temperatures; this choice claims every tropical temperature increase comes with a substantial carbon dioxide increase. Temperatures could rise for other reasons entirely. The word any makes it worse by extending the claim to the smallest temperature uptick while still demanding a substantial change in emissions.

Explanation:
This asks for the main conclusion, so the correct answer is the one claim the essayist is ultimately arguing for. Everything else, however striking, is there to support it. The final sentence is long and contains several claims, so the work is in untangling which part of it is being defended and which part is doing the defending.

Trace the build. The essayist starts with background, that humans have long used myths to explain their place in the cosmos, then draws an analogy, treating science's claims as no different in kind from stories about Homer's gods. Next comes a standard of truth: for science as for myth, truth amounts to how well it helps us cope with the human condition. The final sentence concedes that science has some successes, then states that it falls short of complete truth, and attaches that claim to evidence about science's role in the breakdown of key institutions.

The giveaway is the phrase announcing that something is amply demonstrated by something else. Whatever follows that phrase is the support; whatever precedes it is what the support establishes. So the main conclusion is that science falls short of complete truth, which is to say it is only partially true.
explanation_A: Science's role in the breakdown of key institutions is introduced as the evidence, arriving on the far side of the phrase announcing what demonstrates what. It is the ground, not the thing grounded. Students who simply take the last clause of the last sentence will land here, but position at the end is not a test for a conclusion; the support relation is. Ask which claim is offered as a reason for which, and this one is clearly the reason.
explanation_B: The comparison to Homeric myth appears in the second sentence and sets up the standard of truth the essayist then applies. It is scaffolding for the argument, not its destination. It is also stronger than the verdict actually reached: the essayist grants science some successes and charges it only with falling short of complete truth, which stops well short of ranking it no truer than tales of the gods.
explanation_C: Correct. The final sentence says that science falling short of complete truth is demonstrated by the degree to which science is responsible for institutional breakdown, and that phrasing settles the direction of support. Falling short of complete truth while still counting some successes is exactly what it means to be only partially true, so this choice restates the supported claim rather than the supporting one. Everything earlier feeds it: the myth analogy and the coping standard together make it possible to test science's truth by its social effects, which is what the evidence then purports to do.
explanation_D: Reducing science to mere myth is an overstatement the essayist never endorses. The passage says science resembles myth in a particular respect and is judged by the same standard, and it explicitly credits science with successes. A conclusion has to be something the author actually asserts, and this inflates an analogy into an identity. Watch for answers that take a comparison in one respect and convert it into a claim of sameness.
explanation_E: This captures the opening observation about humans explaining their place in the cosmos, extended to science by the analogy that follows. It is uncontested background, the shared ground from which the argument departs. Nothing in the passage is offered as evidence for it, and no reader is expected to resist it, which is the opposite of what a conclusion requires.

Explanation:
This is a flaw question, so the correct answer has to name the specific defect in how the premises support the conclusion, not a weakness in the recommendation itself.

Track the parts. The conclusion is a prohibition: sodium nitrate should never be added to sausages. The support is that the additive is cosmetic rather than preservative, that excessive use pushes sodium past what taste requires, and that excessive sodium intake can lead to health problems. Notice where the word excessive sits. Every health claim in the stimulus attaches to excessive use, but the conclusion bans the additive outright, including modest amounts that would never push sodium past the taste threshold.

Before reading the choices, expect something about the jump from curbing overuse to forbidding all use. The argument never explains why the most drastic available remedy is required when a limit on quantity would remove the very harm it identified.
explanation_A: Sampling is the wrong diagnosis here. The argument cites no study, survey or collection of cases from which it generalizes; it reasons instead from general claims about what sodium nitrate does and what excessive sodium causes. You cannot fault evidence as unrepresentative when none of it was drawn from a sample in the first place.
explanation_B: Risks created by the recommendation would matter if removing nitrate introduced some new hazard, and a student may reach for this because a blanket ban does sound drastic. But the stimulus heads that worry off by telling you the additive contributes nothing to preventing spoilage, so the obvious downside of dropping it is already accounted for. The real gap concerns the size of the remedy, not its side effects.
explanation_C: Government action and consent appear nowhere in this reasoning. The argument recommends what should be done about an additive; it never says who would enforce that, and it never assumes authority to override anyone's choices. This choice imports a paternalism objection that the argument simply does not depend on.
explanation_D: Correct. Every health claim offered covers only excessive use: too much sodium nitrate pushes sodium beyond what good taste needs, and excessive sodium can lead to health problems. That evidence supports restricting how much is added. The conclusion instead rules out adding any at all, and the argument gives you nothing to close that distance, no reason why a cap on quantity would fail to protect anyone. Preferring the most extreme fix when the evidence condemns only overuse is exactly the unjustified step this choice names.
explanation_E: Check for the two kinds of justification being contrasted and you will find only one of them present. The case here is entirely medical: excessive sodium leads to health problems. Cost, profit and market considerations never enter the stimulus, so there is no economic justification available to be blurred with the medical one.

Explanation:
This is a must-be-true question. The correct answer has to follow from combining the statements; a claim that merely could be true, however plausible it sounds, is wrong.

Sort the claims before you read on. Being well run is stated as necessary for a zoo to make a valuable contribution, so a valuable contribution gives you well run and never the reverse. Large plus well run gives you some full-time veterinarians. You are also told that many small well-run zoos have only part-time veterinarians, that many large zoos both make valuable contributions and stay open all year, and that most small zoos close in winter.

That second-to-last group is the one to chain. Those large zoos make valuable contributions, so they are well run; being large and well run, they have full-time veterinarians; and they are open all year by stipulation. Expect a modest existential claim linking year-round operation to full-time veterinary staff.
explanation_A: A majority claim about large zoos overshoots the count you were given. The stimulus says many large zoos make valuable contributions, and many is not most; it establishes that such zoos exist without telling you what share of all large zoos they represent. Nothing in the statements converts an indefinite quantity into a majority.
explanation_B: This hardens the veterinary rule into something stronger than what was stated. Large well-run zoos have some full-time veterinarians, which tells you what they must have, not what they are forbidden to have. A zoo can employ full-time and part-time veterinarians at the same time. Students pick this by reading some full-time as only full-time, and that single substitution is what makes the claim unsupported.
explanation_C: The strongest trap in the set. You do know that many small well-run zoos have only part-time veterinarians, and the pull is to assume those zoos must be contributing something valuable to their communities. But the stimulus runs that conditional in the opposite direction: making a valuable contribution requires being well run, so being well run does not by itself deliver a valuable contribution. Meeting a necessary condition is not meeting the whole requirement.
explanation_D: Correct, and the chain is short. Many large zoos make valuable contributions to their communities and are open all year. Making a valuable contribution requires being well run, so those zoos are well run. They are also large, and every large well-run zoo has some full-time veterinarians on staff. The same zoos are therefore both open all year and staffed with full-time veterinarians, which is all this choice asserts. The weak existential some is exactly the strength the premises license.
explanation_E: What the stimulus tells you about small zoos concerns their winter hours: most are closed. Whether they contribute anything valuable to their communities is never addressed, and the only other small-zoo fact given concerns part-time veterinary staffing. Since being well run is merely necessary for a valuable contribution, even the well-run small zoos cannot be counted as contributors, let alone most small zoos.

Explanation:
This is a flaw question, so the answer must identify the gap between what the principal established and what the principal concluded.

Lay the pieces out. All rural students take part in the lunch program; roughly half the urban students do as well. Some participants in that program, including some of the strongest academic achievers, also take part in extracurricular activities. The conclusion then splits that overlap two ways: some extracurricular participants are rural and some are urban.

Watch what the word some will and will not carry. Saying that some lunch-program participants also do extracurriculars tells you the overlap is not empty; it says nothing whatever about who populates it. Every student in that overlap could be rural, or every one of them could be urban, and all the premises would remain true. The principal treats mixed membership as given when the evidence guarantees only membership.
explanation_A: No headcount comparison involving strong academic achievers appears anywhere in the argument. They are mentioned once, as an aside about who the participants include, and the conclusion says nothing about them at all. Even if the comparison were assumed, it would do nothing to show that both rural and urban students appear among extracurricular participants.
explanation_B: Close to the real problem, but framed as a comparison the argument never needs. The principal does not require rural participants to outnumber urban ones; the conclusion claims only that each group has at least one member in extracurricular activities. Assuming a larger rural share would not be the error, and denying it would leave the conclusion exactly as unsupported as it already is.
explanation_C: Correct. The only bridge from the lunch program to extracurricular activities is the claim that some program participants also take part in them, and some is silent about composition. The students doing both could be entirely rural, or entirely urban, without contradicting a single premise. By concluding that both kinds are represented, the principal rules out a possibility the evidence leaves wide open, and that is precisely the oversight described here.
explanation_D: How students otherwise occupy their time has no bearing on the inference being drawn. The conclusion concerns who sits inside the extracurricular group, and alternative pastimes would at most explain why certain students stay out of it. Put the argument in a world where extracurriculars were the only option going and it would be just as flawed.
explanation_E: Equivocation is worth testing here, since the word participate covers both the lunch program and extracurricular activities, and this is the choice students reach for when they sense something slippery. But the word carries the same meaning in both uses, taking part in an organized school activity. The slip lies in the quantity word some, not in any shift in what participate denotes.

Explanation:
This is a principle-application question, so the correct answer must supply the facts that make the stated principle actually deliver the stated verdict. Read the principle as a list of conditions, then check which of them the application leaves unestablished.

The principle grants a right to one particular person: the author of an article that appeared in a magazine, who may respond in that magazine. The criticism must either have been published in that same magazine, or published elsewhere and be unfair. The application wants McFinton to respond in Speculator's Digest, and the only fact it offers is that Wallace's article harshly criticizes McFinton's essay.

Two things are therefore missing: that McFinton's essay appeared in Speculator's Digest, which is what entitles him to that magazine's pages, and where Wallace's criticism was published. Expect an answer that nails down both venues at once.
explanation_A: Placing McFinton's essay in Speculator's Digest supplies one half of what the principle demands, which is why this looks promising. The other half never arrives: you still do not know where Wallace's criticism ran. If it appeared in some other magazine, the principle additionally requires that the criticism be unfair, and nothing here or in the application says it is. Half the conditions is not justification.
explanation_B: Here the venue gets pinned down for the wrong article. Knowing that Wallace's criticism appeared in Speculator's Digest accomplishes nothing unless McFinton is an author whose article appeared there, because the principle grants a response only in the magazine that carried the author's own piece. McFinton's essay could have run anywhere at all, and the application would fall apart.
explanation_C: This arrangement actively blocks the application. With McFinton's essay confined to Speculator's Digest and Wallace's criticism spread across other magazines, you land on the principle's second branch, which requires the criticism to be unfair. Nothing here establishes unfairness. Harsh and unfair are not the same property, and the principle insists on the second one.
explanation_D: Correct. Put both articles in Speculator's Digest and every condition closes. McFinton becomes the author of an article that appeared in that magazine, which is what gives him standing to respond in its pages at all. Wallace's harsh criticism of that essay was published in the very same magazine, which satisfies the principle's first branch, so the question of unfairness never needs to be raised. The principle then yields exactly the permission the application asserts.
explanation_E: Tempting, because it appears to hand you more than the credited answer does, adding unfairness on top of a shared venue. But look at what is still absent: no statement that McFinton's essay ever appeared in Speculator's Digest. Without that, he is not an author entitled to respond in those pages, and the extra fact about unfairness is wasted anyway, since unfairness only matters on the branch where the criticism ran in a different magazine.

Explanation:
This is a flaw question, and the conclusion under attack is narrow: the paleontologist claims that one particular reason for rejecting the maniraptor theory is misguided. A correct answer must find the weak point in that specific move.

The dissenting biologists withhold acceptance because the oldest known bird fossils predate the oldest known maniraptor fossils by several million years. The paleontologist replies that the absence of older maniraptor fossils hardly rules out their existence. True enough, but notice the standard that reply quietly assumes. It treats a theory as unreasonable to reject unless the evidence positively forecloses it.

The biologists were never claiming foreclosure. Their point is that the evidence gathered so far does not support the theory, and declining to accept a theory on that basis can be perfectly reasonable. Expect an answer about the distance between not ruled out and adequately supported.
explanation_A: The paleontologist never concludes that birds did evolve from maniraptors; he says only that one argument against the theory misfires. Because he does not assert the theory's truth, the observation that a theory can still be false even when objections to it fail lands on a claim he never made.
explanation_B: Read this carefully and it works in the paleontologist's favour rather than against him. If maniraptors could have existed before birds without leaving fossils older than the oldest bird fossils, that is one more reason the fossil gap settles nothing, which is precisely his point. A criticism has to expose a weakness; this observation reinforces the position it is meant to undermine.
explanation_C: Proof is a far stronger notion than anything the paleontologist invokes. He raises only the possibility that older maniraptor fossils exist, and he uses that possibility to neutralize an objection rather than to establish descent. Attributing to him the view that such fossils would settle the matter misstates what his argument actually rests on.
explanation_D: Evidence of other kinds lies outside what he set out to address. His target is a single line of reasoning built on fossil ages, and he can rebut that line without first surveying everything else that might bear on the question. A student drawn here is holding him to a conclusion about the theory's truth that he never reached.
explanation_E: Correct. The paleontologist's entire reply rests on the fact that missing fossils do not rule out the theory, and he treats that fact as enough to convict the dissenting biologists of misguided reasoning. But their position was never that the theory is impossible; it was that the evidence discovered so far, which places birds ahead of maniraptors in the fossil record, falls short of supporting it. Refusing to accept a theory on the grounds that the available evidence appears insufficient can be entirely reasonable, and he never engages with that possibility.

explanation_A: This points to confusion among the public and says the arguments were hard for most people to evaluate. The passage never discusses how anyone received or assessed these arguments until its final clause, and that clause reports only that the views were not widely accepted, with no explanation involving difficulty of evaluation. Nor does the passage describe conflicting ideas about universal individual rights; the conflict it describes is between two strategies for securing women's rights, both proceeding from the same revolutionary commitment.
explanation_B: Here the claim is that the two positions turn out to be more alike than they first appear. That is the reverse of what the first paragraph asserts, where the two arguments are called radically opposed courses of action, and nothing later softens that. The body of the passage widens the gap rather than closing it, contrasting theory with activism and inevitability with struggle. A main point choice cannot invert the passage's central framing.
explanation_C: Two things go wrong. The absence of specific legislative proposals is attributed only to Condorcet, in the sentence that opens the last paragraph; Gouges is presented as working from concrete details and naming concrete demands. The choice also manufactures a causal link, treating the lack of legislation as the reason the views were not accepted. The passage reports the lack of acceptance as a bare historical fact and offers no cause for it at all.
explanation_D: Correct. This is a main point question, so you want the claim the whole passage is organized to deliver, not a detail from one paragraph. The first paragraph states it directly: Condorcet and Gouges both supported rights for women, but Condorcet held that those rights would follow from the establishment of universal equal rights and so needed no vigorous political action, while Gouges held that women's political inequality was the wellspring of their other injustices and had to be fought directly. The second and third paragraphs do nothing but develop each half of that contrast in turn, which is exactly the shape this choice describes.
explanation_E: The Condorcet half is roughly defensible, since he expected the inequality to disappear soon on its own. The Gouges half is invented. Nowhere does the passage have her tie success to the Revolution still raging; her point about the Revolution is the opposite complaint, that women's political rights remained limited after it. Watch for choices that pair one accurate clause with one fabricated clause, since the accurate clause is what makes them tempting.

explanation_A: Correct. This is an EXCEPT question about stated detail, so four choices appear in the passage as things Gouges counted on and one does not. Revolutionary universalism is the item she attacks rather than relies on: the last paragraph has her exposing harmful inconsistencies in the period's revolutionary universalism, noting that women's political rights were still limited after the Revolution. In other words, the universalist rhetoric is the thing that failed women, which is precisely why she thought direct political action was necessary. Treating it as an aid reverses her relationship to it.
explanation_B: Political involvement is the core of her program, so this one is supported and therefore not the answer. The passage says her proposals aimed at getting women politically mobilized, and that only the political vigilance of women could prevent men from appropriating the benefits of the Revolution. Her closing demand is for full political rights. On an EXCEPT question, confirm each supported item quickly and move on rather than weighing which is best.
explanation_C: Equal access to property appears explicitly in the list of things Gouges said women needed before their disadvantage in dealings with men would end. Since the passage names it as part of what she was arguing for, it counts as something she believed would aid women in achieving equality, which makes it a supported item and not the exception the stem is after.
explanation_D: Direct action is how the first paragraph characterizes her entire approach, in contrast to Condorcet: the political inequalities women faced should be battled through direct political action. The last paragraph reinforces it with the language of war and mobilization. This is as firmly stated as anything in the passage, so it cannot be the item she failed to endorse.
explanation_E: Public employment sits in the same closing list as full political rights and equal access to property, named as part of what would be required before women's ubiquitous disadvantage would end. Because the passage attributes that demand to Gouges directly, the choice is supported and is therefore eliminated on an EXCEPT question.

explanation_A: This gets the adversarial framing right but attaches the wrong reason and drops half the scope. The passage has men stubbornly perpetuating injustices, not men refusing reasonable discussion; the idea that the problem is a failure of reasoning belongs to Condorcet, not Gouges. This choice also confines the struggle to an unspecified arena, leaving out the private disadvantage in marriage that the passage explicitly includes.
explanation_B: Notice the widening in the middle of this choice. Extending the struggle to women and all others who are disempowered turns Gouges into a theorist of general equality, which is Condorcet's move rather than hers. Her distinctive claim is that women's political inequality is a specific wellspring with specific effects on women, and she develops her argument from the details of what women experience. The generalization is what kills this choice.
explanation_C: Correct. The stem asks you to summarize Gouges's position on how equal rights get extended, so you need both the method and its target. The method is a political struggle waged by women, which the passage gives as direct political action, mobilization, and the vigilance needed to stop men from appropriating the Revolution's benefits. The target is men's position of power across every arena: the passage says the prevailing political inequality disadvantaged women in all their dealings with men, and names marriage among them alongside property and public employment. That pairing of public and private is exactly what this choice captures and what the other options miss.
explanation_D: The first half is fine; the second half has no basis anywhere in the passage. Allies, and specifically sympathetic men in positions of power, are never mentioned. The passage presents men as the party whose appropriation of the Revolution's benefits Gouges wanted women's vigilance to prevent, which cuts against the idea of recruiting them. When a choice adds a strategic element the text never raises, treat the addition as disqualifying.
explanation_E: Right idea, wrong person. Treating equal rights for women as an inevitable consequence rather than something won by direct action is Condorcet's position, stated in the first paragraph and developed in the second, where he concludes the inequality is historically condemned to disappear soon. Gouges is defined by her rejection of exactly that expectation, so this choice hands her the view she was arguing against.

explanation_A: Gouges really was a supporter of the Revolution, and the first paragraph says so outright. That is what makes this tempting and also what sinks it: a fact the passage states plainly elsewhere does not need martial vocabulary to convey it, and the two words in question describe how she thought rights would be won, not which side of the Revolution she was on. True, but it answers a question the stem did not ask.
explanation_B: This treats the two words as Gouges's own rallying language quoted back to us. They are the author's descriptions of her position, not samples of anything she wrote or said, and the passage never characterizes her output as propaganda. It describes proposals, arguments, and an exposure of inconsistencies. Attributing the diction to the wrong speaker is the defect here.
explanation_C: Correct. This is a function question about word choice, so ask what the author gains by reaching for violent vocabulary at those two points. Both moments sit at the hinge of Gouges's position: battled describes how she thought women's political inequalities had to be confronted, and war names the campaign she wanted women mobilized into against injustices men were perpetuating. The surrounding content is all about power, with men appropriating the Revolution's benefits and women disadvantaged in every dealing with them. The martial diction marks this as a contest over power rather than a misunderstanding to be corrected, which is exactly the contrast with Condorcet.
explanation_D: Taking war literally produces this choice. Nothing in the passage concerns armed conflict or women serving in it; the campaign Gouges envisioned is political, aimed at rights, property, and public employment. When a question asks about the purpose of a figurative term, the literal reading is almost always planted as a trap, and here it would also require the passage to supply a position it never states.
explanation_E: This has Gouges crediting the Revolution with advancing women's cause. The last paragraph says the opposite: she pointed to harmful inconsistencies in revolutionary universalism and observed that women's political rights remained limited after the Revolution. Her fighting language exists because she thought the Revolution had not delivered for women, so this choice inverts the very dissatisfaction the diction expresses.

explanation_A: This is the strongest wrong answer, because mobilization genuinely is part of her program. But the reason it offers is a mismatch of numbers, as though marriage were a poor target simply for involving two people rather than a group. The passage grounds her ordering in causation, not scale: political inequality is the wellspring, and the disadvantage inside marriage is one of its downstream effects. Swap the causal reason for a logistical one and the choice stops being hers.
explanation_B: Resistance to changing traditional institutions is a plausible real-world thought that the passage simply never voices. Marriage appears once, as an example of the dealings with men in which political inequality disadvantaged women. No claim is made about tradition, social acceptance, or how hard particular institutions are to reform, so this reason has to be imported from outside.
explanation_C: Equal access to property does appear in Gouges's list of demands, which is why this feels anchored. The passage never says marriage is inherently unequal without shared property, though, and more importantly the claim would not answer the stem. Even if true, it gives no reason to think marriage is a bad place to start rather than a good one. Being derived from the right paragraph is not the same as answering the question asked.
explanation_D: Correct. The stem asks for an inference about strategic ordering, so find the sentence that makes one kind of inequality prior to the others. The last paragraph supplies it: Gouges held that women's political inequality was not just another form of inequality but the source of their unequal position in society, and that the resulting disadvantage in all their dealings with men, marriage explicitly included, would continue until women held full political rights. If marital inequality is an effect of political inequality, attacking marriage first treats the symptom and leaves the cause untouched. Political equality has to come first.
explanation_E: This sentence belongs to Condorcet. The first paragraph assigns him the view that women's rights are a specific instance of rights in general, and the second explains why that led him away from targeted political action. Gouges's whole contribution is the denial of it, insisting women's political inequality is a distinct source rather than a special case. The choice also would not explain any preference about where to begin.

explanation_A: Property shows up only on Gouges's side, in her list of what women needed, and even there the passage records the demand rather than any account of how women might come to own property. Since the stem requires something both figures raised, a point made by one of them, and incompletely at that, cannot qualify.
explanation_B: Correct. The stem asks what both arguments share, so look for a single idea each paragraph attributes to its own subject. Inconsistency is that idea. Condorcet's paragraph grounds his entire case in it, treating all discrimination as an oversight arising from not reasoning consistently, so that continued inequality is intellectually untenable. Gouges's paragraph has her exposing harmful inconsistencies in the period's revolutionary universalism, pointing out that women's political rights stayed limited even after a revolution proclaiming universal rights. The two draw opposite strategic conclusions from the observation, but both build on the charge that people were holding beliefs that do not hang together.
explanation_C: The opening of the last paragraph rules this out explicitly, noting that Condorcet's arguments were purely theoretical and included no specific legislative proposals. Since one of the two is stated not to have taken this up, the choice fails the both requirement immediately. Checking each candidate against the weaker of the two figures is the fastest way through a question like this.
explanation_D: This is Condorcet's thesis, and it is the thesis Gouges rejects. She held that women's political inequality was not just another form of inequality but the source of women's unequal position, which is the direct denial of treating women's rights as indistinguishable from rights in general. A point one figure asserts and the other contradicts is the opposite of common ground.
explanation_E: Limits on governmental power never enter the passage. The discussion concerns equal rights, reasoning, political mobilization, and access to property and employment, not constraints on what government may do. Neither figure is described as making this argument, so there is nothing to attribute to either of them, let alone to both.

explanation_A: This is Passage B's thesis, not a shared one. Gumbrecht's argument about beauty and apparent purposiveness just is the claim that athletic performances can be appreciated aesthetically. Passage A never goes there: its sport is ceremony plus skill judged by informed fans, and beauty plays no part in the defense. On a comparative purpose question you lose on the half you did not check, so test every candidate against Passage A before you accept it.
explanation_B: Ceremony appears only in Passage A, and even there the point is that ceremony requires witnesses, not that sport matches art in ceremonial function. Passage B says nothing about ritual or ceremony at all. The choice also misreads Passage A, which contrasts the two audiences rather than ranking the two kinds of performance on some ceremonial scale.
explanation_C: Passage A does hold that athletic excellence is relatively uncontroversial as a judgment, so half of this feels earned. Passage B, though, never claims sport is judged by well-defined standards; Kant's purposiveness explains why something strikes us as beautiful, not what criteria anyone applies. A claim that fits one passage and is absent from the other cannot be a principal purpose of both.
explanation_D: Correct. The question asks for a purpose the two passages share, so the answer has to be abstract enough to cover two fairly different arguments. Setting the evaluation of athletic performance beside the evaluation of artistic performance does exactly that. Passage A devotes its second paragraph to the discriminating sports public versus an art audience adrift among shifting standards, and Passage B's entire case is that the aesthetic judgment we reserve for the concert hall and the museum belongs to a well-played game too. Opposite verdicts, identical comparison.
explanation_E: Audience knowledge is genuinely Passage A's engine, and its contrast with art audiences is explicit. The trouble is Passage B, which is concerned with what academics refuse to see, not with how much fans know. Even within Passage A this is a supporting contrast rather than the overarching purpose. Watch for choices that are accurate about one passage and simply silent about the other.

explanation_A: Correct. This asks you to locate an item present in one passage and absent from the other, so the work is mechanical. When Passage B reaches Kant's paradox it names two sports outright, pointing to a triple axel in figure skating and a double play in baseball as actions with no function outside their games. Passage A discusses sport only in the abstract, as games, athletic contests and the sporting public, and never names a single one. The asymmetry runs in the direction the question requires.
explanation_B: No award for artistic excellence turns up anywhere. Passage A discusses standards of excellence and their erosion, and Passage B discusses aesthetic appeal, but neither brings in a prize, honor or competition. An item absent from both passages cannot satisfy a question that demands presence in one and absence in the other.
explanation_C: Artistic disciplines do appear, but on the wrong side of the ledger. Passage A lists amateur musicians, dancers, actors and painters, so this item sits in the passage the question wants it absent from. Passage B gestures only at the concert hall and the museum, which name venues rather than disciplines. The direction is reversed, and that reversal is the whole trap.
explanation_D: No athlete is named. The passages do supply proper names, Gumbrecht and Kant in B and Podhoretz in A, so a quick scan that registers only that B is full of names can make this look plausible. All of them are thinkers, though, and the maneuvers Passage B describes are generic moves anyone in the sport might perform rather than feats by a particular competitor.
explanation_E: A particular moment from the history of sports would be a dated event, a named final or a record broken. Passage B supplies nothing of the kind: a triple axel and a double play are recurring types of play, used to illustrate apparent purposiveness. The pull comes from Gumbrecht's talk of great moments in sport, but that phrase is as general as the examples under it.

explanation_A: Ranking sports against one another never happens. Passage B does set figure skating beside baseball, which can momentarily read as a comparison, but the two are offered as parallel illustrations of the same point about apparent purposiveness, with no hint that either is the finer sport.
